#### Running Tasks

##### Description

The header heads the view with every task under way, not only the latest, that is the latest task, and every other task building, compiling, or running, as when a Spec task and a Code task run in their two lanes at once, or a chain's step runs beside a task of the other lane. Only one of them is selected at a time, and only it is shown in full, with its header as a task's header always is, its compiled prompt, hidden anchor's name, status label and elapsed time, and buttons, and beneath it its output table and the files it changed. The others are compact rows, one each, stacked above the selected task's header, in the order they were sent, oldest at the top. With only one task to show, there are no compact rows, and the header is just as it was.

##### Compact Row

A compact row is one line, 28 pixels tall, across the view's full width, on a faint tint of its task's mode's colour, as a previous task's heading is tinted, with a thin line in the theme's line colour between one row and the next and beneath the last. From left to right, 8 pixels in: its status label and elapsed time, as every task's are, then the first line of its prompt, as it was typed, in small text, cut off with an ellipsis, then, at its right, its Cancel button while it is under way, as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) gives every task one, and nothing else: no compiled prompt, no hidden anchor's name, no Resend or Send to the other mode, no output, and no changed files. Its tooltip gives the prompt's first lines and the mode it was sent in. Hovering it shows the theme's hover over the tint.

##### Selecting

Clicking a compact row, anywhere but its Cancel button, selects its task, which takes the full form, in its place beneath the compact rows, and the task selected before becomes a compact row, in its own place in the order sent, the switch made at once, without a slide. Each task's output keeps how far it was scrolled, and whether its lock to the bottom was on, while another is selected, so selecting it again shows it just as it was left, locked tables showing all that arrived meanwhile. The selected task's header keeps its mode's colour, as the latest task's always has, and the [RightSidebarScope](../../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar-scope) shows the selected task's referenced spec, understanding, and subagents while it runs, and the other running task's once it has finished while another still runs.
A newly sent task, once it starts building, is selected, as the latest task always has been, the one selected before becoming a compact row. Otherwise the selection stays where it was put: a task finishing doesn't move it. A task other than the latest that finishes leaves the header for the previous tasks as soon as it isn't selected, there showing as any finished task does; one finishing while selected stays, in full, until another is selected, and then leaves. The latest task always stays, compact or in full, finished or not, as it always heads the view. Each open project keeps its own selection, as it keeps the rest of its message list.

##### Previous Tasks

A task in the header, compact or in full, is not among the previous tasks, and isn't counted in their row, which counts every task but those the header shows. Once it leaves the header, it is among them as any task is.

#### Scrolling

##### Description

The latest task's table scrolls with its lock to the bottom off to start with, until switched on. Each open project keeps how far its latest task's table was scrolled and whether it was locked, and the rest of its message list as it was left, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says, so switching back to it shows the list just as it was.
However long the list of previous tasks grows, drawing it costs no more than drawing the tasks in view, so scrolling, animations, and new output stay smooth.

##### Scrolling Past

The previous tasks are not above the latest task in the message list but in the right sidebar's Tasks tab, so nothing lies past either end of the selected task's output: scrolling stops at its top and its bottom, with no stretch, glow, or crossing over. A task opened from the Tasks tab opens in a tab of its own, never in the Chat tab, so the selected task's output stays scrolled just where it was left.

#### Changed Files

Otherwise the selection stays where it was put: a task finishing doesn't move it. A task other than the latest that finishes leaves the header for the previous tasks as soon as it isn't selected, there showing as any finished task does; one finishing while selected stays, in full, until another is selected, and then leaves. The latest task always stays, compact or in full, finished or not, as it always heads the view. Each open project keeps its own selection, as it keeps the rest of its message list.

##### Previous Tasks

A task in the header, compact or in full, is not among the previous tasks, and isn't counted in their row, which counts every task but those the header shows. Once it leaves the header, it is among them as any task is.

#### Scrolling

##### Description

The latest task's table scrolls with its lock to the bottom off to start with, until switched on. Each open project keeps how far its latest task's table was scrolled and whether it was locked, and the rest of its message list as it was left, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says, so switching back to it shows the list just as it was.
However long the list of previous tasks grows, drawing it costs no more than drawing the tasks in view, so scrolling, animations, and new output stay smooth.

##### Scrolling Past

The previous tasks are not above the latest task in the message list but in the right sidebar's Tasks tab, so nothing lies past either end of the selected task's output: scrolling stops at its top and its bottom, with no stretch, glow, or crossing over. A task opened from the Tasks tab opens in a tab of its own, never in the Chat tab, so the selected task's output stays scrolled just where it was left.

content.content:
#### Logging In

When the harness isn't logged in, in its volume, the application runs its login command in a container, under a pseudo-terminal, and shows a login view in an inset panel, titled for the harness, with what the command prints. The login URL the command prints opens in the host's browser, once, and nothing else ever opens one.
Only the login command's own output is read for it, from when the command starts, never what the image build prints before it, nor anything Podman prints while it pulls, builds, or starts the container, all of which is shown as text and never opened, its URLs at most clickable links. And only a URL that is the harness's login is opened: the first one the login command prints that leads to its sign-in, as Claude Code's to claude.ai or console.anthropic.com, Codex's to auth.openai.com, or OpenCode's to the provider it is logging in with, or a localhost callback it asks to be visited. Any other URL it prints, as a link to documentation, release notes, or a package's homepage, is only shown. A login opens at most one URL by itself, the first such one; any later is shown as a link, for the user to click. Where no URL is recognized, nothing opens, and the view shows every URL the command printed as a link instead.
Where the command asks for a code to be pasted, the view has a field for it, and what is entered there goes to the command. Where the command waits for a callback on a known localhost port, that port is published for the login run. Where it offers to log in with a device code, that is how it logs in. The run waiting on the login is sent once the login succeeds, and fails, saying so, if it is cancelled or fails.
A login needs the image, as any run in a container does, and the first login on a machine is most often the first thing to need it. So the login view builds it first where it isn't there or is out of date, showing "Preparing environment" and what the build prints as it goes, and starts the login command only once the build has succeeded. A build that fails shows why in the login view, as a failed build says it, with a "Try again" button that builds it again, and starts no login.
The harness's volume is ready for it before its first login: created by the application with `podman volume create` where it isn't there, and mounted so that the user the container runs as owns it and can write it, as with Podman's `:U` option, never left owned by root where the harness runs as the user. The container's HOME, where the volume is mounted beneath it, as ~/.claude, is a directory that user owns, as is the volume, so the login command can write its credentials there on the first login as on any other.
Which harness is logged in is always the one the run needs: the harness of the run's project, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, never Claude Code by default, and never another project's. A run, a Welcome check, or a login asked for checks that harness's own volume alone, by its own credentials file: Claude Code's `~/.claude/.credentials.json`, Codex's `~/.codex/auth.json`, and OpenCode's `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`, each counting as logged in only where the file is there and not empty. Its login view is titled for it, "Log in to Codex" and the like, and runs its own login command, `claude /login` for Claude Code, `codex login` for Codex, and `opencode auth login` for OpenCode, in a container with that harness's volume mounted, so its credentials land where its runs read them. A run never asks for one harness's login while it is about to run another.
A run that fails because its harness isn't logged in says so, naming the harness, "Codex isn't logged in", with a "Log in" button that shows its login view, rather than the harness's raw error alone. A login that fails says why in the command's own words, its exit status, and which harness it was for, and the run waiting on it fails saying the same. The login view, the Welcome check, and the Settings rows all read the same volume for a harness, so a harness that is logged in shows as logged in everywhere, and one that isn't never shows as logged in anywhere.
The credentials stay in the harness's volume, and are refreshed there, so a harness is logged in once on a machine, not for every run. The [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope) shows whether each harness is logged in in its container, and can log it in again.

#### Guards
#### Volumes

The only volumes are one per harness, for its login and settings, ~/.claude, ~/.codex, or OpenCode's data directory as the harness keeps it, owned and named by the application and shared by every project, so each harness is logged in once for all of them. Losing one costs only a login.
The harness's sessions are never kept in a volume. They are kept in the project, in `.suspense/sessions/`, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, one folder per conversation: `spec` for the spec lane's, and `questions` for the Ask tab's questions. Each run mounts only its own conversation's folder, read and write, where the harness keeps its sessions under its home, as Claude Code's ~/.claude/projects, never `.suspense/sessions/` as a whole, so no run sees another conversation's sessions. The application creates the folder before the run if it isn't there. So a conversation carries on across runs, restarts of the application, and moves of the project, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says.
Losing the project's sessions folder costs only the conversations'

##### Context

the next run starts a new conversation, as when a session

can't be resumed. Sessions kept in volumes before this aren't carried over; each conversation starts fresh.

#### Logging In

If the project still asks for Claude Code, check its harness in Settings › Agent. A project with no saved harness uses the first agent in its `piton.config.pi`, which may be Claude Code.

content.content:
#### Image

Runs use an image the application builds itself, with `podman build`, and keeps up to date: the default image, holding the harness commands, Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, and piton, each at the version installed on the host where it can be found there, and at its latest otherwise. It is built again when any of those versions changes.
Each command the image holds has to run in it, not only be there. The build ends by running each one's version command in the image, as `piton --version`, and a build where one fails, as a piton built against a newer C library than the image has, fails, saying which command couldn't run and what it printed. An image whose piton can't run is never used, so a Spec run is never sent where it can't run `piton build` to check its work.
A project can add to it with a Containerfile of its own, `.suspense/Containerfile`, built FROM the default image, to add what its runs in a container need, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says. The project's image is built from it, and kept, and built again only when the Containerfile or the default image changes. Without one, the project's runs use the default image.
While an image is being built for a run, the task or question shows "Preparing environment" as its status, and what the build prints goes to its raw output. A build that fails fails the run, saying why.
The image is a Linux image, whatever the host is, so what it holds is installed in it for Linux, for the architecture Podman runs: each harness and piton at the version found on the host, from its own Linux release or package, never a binary copied from the host, which on macOS or Windows can't run in it. The build is given only the Containerfile the application writes for it, in a build context of its own, a fresh temporary directory holding nothing else, never the project or the user's home, and needs nothing from the host but the network.
Each harness is installed in a step of its own, so one that can't be installed never stops the others. A version taken from the host is used only once the package registry is asked, before the build, and has it, as `npm view <package>@<version> version` answering it; the version a host's command prints is read only as a plain version number, never with anything printed around it. A version the registry doesn't have, one that can't be read, or one not published for Linux, is installed at its latest instead, never failing the build, and the welcome page and the Settings' Containers section say which harness runs a different version in its container than on the host, muted, never as an error. A harness that can't be installed at all is left out of the image, which still builds, and only runs that need it fail, as below.
Only one build of an image runs at a time. A run, a login, or a welcome or settings check that needs an image already being built waits for that build and shares how it ended, rather than starting another, so two builds never race to tag the same image. A build is tagged only once it has succeeded, so a build that fails or is interrupted never leaves an image that is taken for a good one, and the next need of it builds it again.
A build that fails, or a harness left out of it, is never shown as a wall of Podman's output. The run, the login view, or the welcome check shows a short message in plain words saying what went wrong and what can be done, with a button for each fix the application can make itself, then, collapsed beneath a "Details" disclosure, the step it failed at and everything the build printed, as written, and the same is kept in the debug log. So a package version that doesn't exist reads "OpenCode 2.0.14 isn't available to install" with "Use the latest OpenCode", which builds again with it at its latest; no network reads "Couldn't download what the container needs: check your internet connection" with "Try again"; Podman out of disk space reads so, with "Free up space", which runs `podman system prune` once confirmed; and anything else reads "The container couldn't be set up" with "Try again" and "Copy details". The message is in the theme's warning colour, not its error colour, while a fix is offered.

#### Mounts
29:- "Harness", the open project's harness, named in the row as "Codex" and the like, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, never Claude Code unless that is the project's, and with no project open, the harness a new project starts with, its row saying so, found by running its command with `--version`, required, since Code tasks run it on the host. Missing, its guidance names the command and links to the harness's installation instructions, https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/setup for Claude Code, https://github.com/openai/codex for Codex, and https://opencode.ai/docs/ for OpenCode, with a "Choose another harness" button that opens the Agent section of the [SettingsWindowScope](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope).
33:- "Harness login", required, named for the same harness as the row above, passing while that harness is logged in in its container, read from its volume. Not logged in, its guidance offers "Log in", which shows the login view, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says. It is checked only once "Containers" passes.
40:"Check again" runs every check anew. The harness checks run anew by themselves whenever another project is opened or the open project's harness is changed, so they never speak of a harness the project doesn't use. A check whose action, as setting up Podman or logging in, finishes runs again by itself, and so do the checks waiting on it. A link opened in the browser leaves the page as it is, until Check again.

Your build failed because the container image pins OpenCode to `opencode-ai@2.0.14`, the version read from your machine, and npm has no such version (its latest is 1.18.35). That one bad version made the single shared install step fail, taking Claude Code and Codex down with it. Each harness now installs on its own, and failures are explained in plain words with buttons to fix them. All tests pass, including new ones, but I haven't run a real image build, login or the Welcome page here.

- **Versions are checked first:** a version read from your machine is used only if `npm view <package>@<version> version` confirms npm has it. Otherwise that harness installs at its latest. Only a plain version number is taken from what your machine's command prints.
- **One harness can't break the others:** each harness gets its own install step, falling back to the latest version and then to leaving it out. A harness left out doesn't fail the build; only runs that need it do.
- **Guidance instead of walls of output:** a failed build now gives a short plain-words message instead of Podman's output:

  | Problem | Message | Buttons |
  |---|---|---|
  | Version not on npm | "OpenCode 2.0.14 isn't available to install" | Use the latest OpenCode |
  | No network | "Couldn't download what the container needs: check your internet connection" | Try again |
  | Podman out of disk space | Says so | Free up space (runs `podman system prune` after you confirm) |
  | Anything else | "The container couldn't be set up" | Try again, Copy details |

  In the login view it's in the warning colour, with Podman's output collapsed under "Details" and also written to the debug log.
- **Welcome:** the harness rows are named for the open project's harness, such as "Codex" and "Codex login". With no project open, the row says it's for new projects. The checks run again when you open another project.
- **Version differences:** if a harness runs a different version in its container than on your machine, Welcome and Settings' Containers section note it in muted text, not as an error.

Places this falls short of the spec:
- **Failed runs:** a run that fails on the build shows the short message as an ordinary error row, offering only the main fix as its button. The Details are in its raw output and the debug log rather than a collapsible section.
- **Changing the harness in Settings:** Welcome re-checks immediately when you open another project. After changing the open project's harness, it re-checks the next time the Welcome page redraws, not instantly.
- **"Use the latest":** this choice lasts only until Suspense restarts. After that, the npm check prevents the bad version from coming back anyway.

49:Each step runs in the lane of the work it does, as the [PromptSendingScope](./sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says: the Chain task and its spec follow-up in the spec lane, the code step in the code lane. A step is sent once the step before it finishes, never before, and takes its place in its lane's queue by when its chain was sent, not when the step itself was: behind every prompt waiting there that was sent before its chain, earlier chains' steps included, and ahead of every prompt sent after it. So a chain's code step never jumps ahead of a Code prompt, or another chain's code step, sent before the chain was, and a Code prompt sent while the chain's spec step ran waits for the chain's code step rather than coming between the chain's steps. Two steps whose chains were sent in the same order run in that order, whichever spec step finished first. Where nothing sent before its chain is waiting, it runs as soon as its lane is free, and straight away if it already is. Its place holds however it came to be queued, so a restart, with the queue read back from the project, keeps it there. The lane it leaves is free for its own queue meanwhile, so a Spec task sent while a chain's code step runs runs beside it. A step waiting for its lane shows in the queue like any prompt, and can be cancelled there, ending the chain. A step whose chain step before it failed or was cancelled is never sent.
51:In the previous tasks list, a chain's steps are grouped under one parent item, so they read as parts of a single chain. The parent is a heading row in the list, tinted the Chain colour, as the [PromptModesScope](./modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it, a little more strongly than a single task's tint: a joined chain icon, the first line of the prompt, and at its right how many steps it has, "2 steps" or "3 steps". Its status is its right how many steps it has, "2 steps" or "3 steps". Its status is the chain's as a whole, worked out only from its steps as they actually are, never from what the chain might still do: Running, with its spinner and its time counting, exactly while one of its steps is building, compiling, or running now, in this project's runs, and at no other time. Otherwise, while one of its steps waits in a lane's queue, it reads Queued, in the theme's muted colour, and is listed with the queued prompts. Otherwise it is over, whether or not it ever sent every step it might have: Failed or Cancelled if a step was, and otherwise its last step's own status, Done, or Not recorded for one with no record of its run. A chain whose later step was never sent, as one from before chains sent them or one whose application closed between its steps, is over, its parent saying muted after its step count that its code step was never sent, and never reads Running for it.
52:Each step's state is read from where it truly is: a step is running only while the application has its run under way, which no step from the history ever does after a restart, since every run ends when the application quits; queued only while its prompt is in the queue; and otherwise from its own history record, a step with no record of its run reading Not recorded, never Running. Steps are joined to their chain only by which step each was sent from, as below, so a task never takes the state of a chain it doesn't belong to, and a chain never counts a task that isn't one of its steps.
53:While a chain is Running, it is listed in the Running group of the right sidebar's Tasks tab, with all its steps beneath it; while Queued, in the Queued group; and once over, among the previous tasks. It has no checkbox, Resend, or Send to the other mode of its own, and clicking it doesn't open anything.
54:Beneath it, each step stays an item of its own, exactly as any previous task is, with its checkbox, status, Resend, and whatever else a task offers, opening onto its own prompt, table, and changed files. The steps are indented from the parent, joined to it by a thin line in the Chain colour down their left, from the parent's heading to the last step, and each is labelled by what it did, "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up", in that step's mode colour, before its prompt, which leaves out the prompt's first line when it is the parent's. They are listed in the order they ran.
55:A chain is listed where its first step was sent, oldest first like every other item; tasks sent while it ran, such as questions or tasks of the other lane run between its steps, are never listed within it, and are listed after the chain, in the order they were sent. A chain's steps are found by which step each was sent from, not by being next to each other in the history. A chain still running, or one whose later steps haven't been sent yet, shows as many steps as have been, and a step still running shows as it would anywhere. When the latest task, heading the view, is a step of a chain, that chain's earlier steps are still grouped under its parent in the list, the parent saying the rest is the latest task. A session divider never falls between a chain's steps: it goes above the chain's parent. A step from the history whose chain can't be worked out, as when the step it was sent from is missing, is listed as a task of its own.
59:The latest task heads the view whether or not the harness is working. It is always the most recent task still active: of the tasks under way, building, compiling, or running, in either lane, the one sent most recently. Only while no task is under way is it the task that finished most recently, or, before any has finished, the one sent most recently. A finished task never heads the view while another is under way: when it finishes while a task in the other lane still runs, that task heads the view in its place at once, and the task that finished goes among the previous tasks. So with two Chain tasks sent one after the other, once both their spec steps have finished, the first chain's code step heads the view while it runs, not the second chain's finished spec step, and the second chain's code step heads it in turn once it is sent. A task still running in the other lane that is not the latest is among the previous tasks, shown running there, as any previous task is. content.content:
#### Status

##### Description

A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green, "Failed" in red, "Cancelled" in orange, and "Not recorded" in grey for a task from the history with no record of its run. The labels are readable in both light and dark mode.

##### Elapsed

Beside its status label, a task shows how long it has been under way, from when it was sent, building and compiling included, in small muted tabular figures: minutes and seconds, "0:42" or "12:05", with hours ahead of them once it reaches an hour, "1:02:33". While the task is building, compiling, or running, it counts up every second, so a task that seems stuck can be told from one that has only just started. Once the task is over, however it ended, it stops and stays at how long the task took. It shows wherever the status label does, the latest task's header and the heading of each previous task, including a task running in the other lane. A task from the history whose record holds no start and end, as one recorded before they were kept, shows how long it took as well as can be told, from the second its history file is named by to when its record was written, with "≈" before it, as "≈ 4:12", its tooltip saying it is approximate; one where neither can be told shows none.
Among the previous tasks, every task's heading shows how long it took, as the latest task's header does, though not beside its status: done, failed, or cancelled alike, and a task still running there counting up. A chain's parent row shows the time its steps took together, from when its first step was sent to when its last ended, and each step's heading beneath it its own. The times line up, right-aligned in their own column of the heading, just before its buttons, so the list reads as a column of durations that can be compared at a glance, and a long one stands out.

#### Running Tasks

content.content:
#### Description

The tab is one scrolling column, with a [ScrollbarScope](../../scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar-scope), read top to bottom as a timeline, in three groups, each headed by a small muted label with its count: "Previous", every task that has run, oldest at the top, as the [PromptEditor](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor)'s previous tasks are, with their filters and batch actions along the group's heading; "Running", every task under way, in either lane; and "Queued", the queue, in its order, as the [QueueListScope](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/queue-list/index.md#queue-list-scope) says, reordered by dragging, its auto-send switch and "Send next" button along its heading. A group with nothing in it shows its heading alone, muted, "No queued prompts" and the like. Each time the tab is shown, it is scrolled so the Running group, or the start of the Queued one when nothing runs, is in view.
The three groups are accordion sections, each collapsible on its own. A section's heading is a row 28 pixels tall, on the theme's raised surface, a step apart from the rows: a chevron at its left, pointing right while collapsed and down while expanded, then its title and count, then, at its right, its own controls, Previous's filter and batch actions and Queued's auto-send switch and "Send next". Clicking the heading, anywhere but its controls, expands or collapses that section alone; any number can be expanded at once, and collapsing one takes its rows away and leaves only its heading. Previous starts collapsed and Running and Queued expanded, each time a project is opened; otherwise each stays as it was left while the application runs, each open project keeping its own. A collapsed section still counts its tasks, its controls still work, and opening one of its tasks from elsewhere, as from the running activity list, expands it to show that task.
Each heading is sticky: while its section's rows are scrolled through, the heading stays pinned at the top of the tab, over the rows scrolling beneath it, until the next section's heading reaches it and pushes it up and out of view, the next one taking its place. So the heading of the section in view is always showing, with its count and controls in reach, however far down it is scrolled. A pinned heading draws over the rows with its own surface, never letting them show through, and is drawn once, never twice where it is pinned and where it lies.

#### Rows

Every task is one row, 28 pixels tall, as a queued prompt's is, and every row in every section is laid out in the same columns, so their parts line up down the whole list: a bar 2 pixels wide down its left edge in its mode's colour, as the [PromptModesScope](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it; then a lead column 20 pixels wide, holding a Previous row's checkbox, a Queued row's drag grip, and nothing in a Running row, the column kept empty rather than closed up where there is nothing in it; then a status column 20 pixels wide, a spinner while it is under way, a tick, cross, or dash once it has ended, or, queued, its place in the queue; then the first line of its prompt, cut off with an ellipsis; then, at its right, muted, how long it took, or has been running, as the [MessageList](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list) writes it, right-aligned in a column of its own, and any buttons the row has after it. So a row's status and its text start at the same place whether it has a checkbox, a grip, or neither, and so do the section headings' titles, set in from their chevrons to line up with the rows' text.
A chain is one row like any other, its status the chain's as a whole, with its step count muted beside its time. Its steps are never listed or expanded in the list; they are shown once it is opened, as its chain steps say. Clicking a row opens it, as below, and the row stays highlighted while it is open. Hovering a row shows its prompt's first lines in its tooltip.

#### Virtualized

The list is virtualized: however many tasks the project has run, it lays out and draws only the rows in view, and a few rows either side of it, never every row, so opening the tab, scrolling it, resizing the sidebar, filtering, and new tasks arriving cost the same with ten thousand previous tasks as with ten. Every row is 28 pixels tall, section headings included, so where each row lies is known from its place in the list alone, without laying out the rows before it, and the scrollbar's thumb is sized and placed from the whole list's height, as though every row were drawn.
A row is drawn only from what its row shows, its mode, status, first line, and time, read from each task's history record once and kept, never by reading a record's output, lines, or snapshots while scrolling; those are read only when a task is opened. Running rows update their time and spinner in place, redrawing only what is in view. Scrolling to a row, as when the tab opens on Running, a filter changes, or a queued row is dragged past the edge, jumps straight to its place without drawing the rows between. A row scrolled out of view and back is the same as it was, its selection and highlight kept. A pinned heading sits over the list without moving any row, so where each row lies is unchanged by it.
Scrolling past either end does nothing: with the list at its top or its bottom, a wheel, trackpad, or drag that goes further leaves every row exactly where it is, frame after frame, with no stretch, bounce, or nudge of even a pixel and back, and draws nothing anew, since nothing moved. Its scroll position is clamped to its ends before a frame is drawn, never drawn past an end and corrected the frame after, and kept in whole device pixels, so a row never shimmers between two places. What lies at an end stays at it: a running row's time ticking, a task finishing, a row added or removed elsewhere in the list, or the tab being resized never makes the rows in view jump and settle. A list scrolled to its bottom stays at its bottom as rows are added, and one at its top stays at its top. The list counts as taller than the tab only once it overflows it by a whole pixel, as the right sidebar's panels do, so a list that fits never scrolls at all.

#### Details
#### Chain Steps

An open Chain task lists its steps beneath its parameters, in the order they run, each a row as in the list, with its status: its spec step, its code step, and its spec follow-up when it has one. An "Add step" button beneath them adds a step of its own after the last: a Code or a Spec step, chosen from a small menu, with a prompt of its own, typed in the step's row as it expands, its model and effort those of the chain until changed. An added step runs once the step before it finishes, in its own mode's lane and place, as every step of a chain does, told its own prompt, the chain's prompt as typed, and what the step before it replied, as the spec-to-code prompt tells a code step, so a chain can be carried on, as a further code change once the spec is built, or a spec tidy-up after the code. A step not yet sent can be edited, moved among the others not yet sent, or removed; one sent reads as it was. Steps are saved with the chain, in its hidden anchor, as the [PromptSendingScope](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) keeps a queued prompt, so a chain keeps its added steps across restarts, and a step whose step before it failed or was cancelled is never sent, as none of a chain's are.

So a row's status and its text start at the same place whether it has a checkbox, a grip, or neither, and so do the section headings' titles, set in from their chevrons to line up with the rows' text.
A chain is one row like any other, its status the chain's as a whole, with its step count muted beside its time. Its steps are never listed or expanded in the list; they are shown once it is opened, as its chain steps say. Clicking a row opens it, as below, and the row stays highlighted while it is open. Hovering a row shows its prompt's first lines in its tooltip.

#### Virtualized

The list is virtualized: however many tasks the project has run, it lays out and draws only the rows in view, and a few rows either side of it, never every row, so opening the tab, scrolling it, resizing the sidebar, filtering, and new tasks arriving cost the same with ten thousand previous tasks as with ten. Every row is 28 pixels tall, section headings included, so where each row lies is known from its place in the list alone, without laying out the rows before it, and the scrollbar's thumb is sized and placed from the whole list's height, as though every row were drawn.
A row is drawn only from what its row shows, its mode, status, first line, and time, read from each task's history record once and kept, never by reading a record's output, lines, or snapshots while scrolling; those are read only when a task is opened. Running rows update their time and spinner in place, redrawing only what is in view. Scrolling to a row, as when the tab opens on Running, a filter changes, or a queued row is dragged past the edge, jumps straight to its place without drawing the rows between. A row scrolled out of view and back is the same as it was, its selection and highlight kept. A pinned heading sits over the list without moving any row, so where each row lies is unchanged by it.
Scrolling past either end does nothing: with the list at its top or its bottom, a wheel, trackpad, or drag that goes further leaves every row exactly where it is, frame after frame, with no stretch, bounce, or nudge of even a pixel and back, and draws nothing anew, since nothing moved. Its scroll position is clamped to its ends before a frame is drawn, never drawn past an end and corrected the frame after, and kept in whole device pixels, so a row never shimmers between two places. What lies at an end stays at it: a running row's time ticking, a task finishing, a row added or removed elsewhere in the list, or the tab being resized never makes the rows in view jump and settle. A list scrolled to its bottom stays at its bottom as rows are added, and one at its top stays at its top. The list counts as taller than the tab only once it overflows it by a whole pixel, as the right sidebar's panels do, so a list that fits never scrolls at all.

#### Details
#### Chain Steps

An open Chain task lists its steps beneath its parameters, in the order they run, each a row as in the list, with its status: its spec step, its code step, and its spec follow-up when it has one. An "Add step" button beneath them adds a step of its own after the last: a Code or a Spec step, chosen from a small menu, with a prompt of its own, typed in the step's row as it expands, its model and effort those of the chain until changed. An added step runs once the step before it finishes, in its own mode's lane and place, as every step of a chain does, told its own prompt, the chain's prompt as typed, and what the step before it replied, as the spec-to-code prompt tells a code step, so a chain can be carried on, as a further code change once the spec is built, or a spec tidy-up after the code. A step not yet sent can be edited, moved among the others not yet sent, or removed; one sent reads as it was. Steps are saved with the chain, in its hidden anchor, as the [PromptSendingScope](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) keeps a queued prompt, so a chain keeps its added steps across restarts, and a step whose step before it failed or was cancelled is never sent, as none of a chain's are.

#### Days

Within Previous, tasks are grouped by the day they were sent, in the user's local time, each day headed by a divider row, 28 pixels tall like every row, its label in small muted text set in to line up with the rows' text: "Today", "Yesterday", the weekday for the rest of the past week, as "Tuesday", and the date beyond that, as "3 October", with the year added once it isn't this one, as "28 September 2025", then, muted after it, how many tasks that day holds. Days run oldest to newest, as the tasks do, and only days with a task are shown; a chain is under the day its first step was sent. While filters are on, a day with no task shown is left out, and its count is of the tasks shown. The labels follow the clock: one reading "Today" reads "Yesterday" once midnight has passed, without reopening the tab.
A day's divider is sticky beneath Previous's own heading: while its tasks are scrolled through, it stays pinned just below that heading, until the next day's divider pushes it out, so the day of the rows in view always shows. Day dividers take the place of the session dividers the previous tasks had; a session that starts a new conversation shows a small muted mark at its first row's right instead, its tooltip saying it started a new conversation.

#### Rows
44:Filtering only hides tasks from the list; it changes nothing about them. A chain whose steps are hidden in part keeps its parent row above the steps still shown, and is hidden with its parent only when none of its steps shows. Day dividers show only above a day with a task shown, as the [TasksTabScope](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/tasks/index.md#tasks-tab-scope) says. The row's count still counts every previous task, and while any option is checked, the Previous group's heading, after its count, reads " · N shown", N counting the previous tasks the filters show. A hidden task stays selected if it was, and is still counted in "N selected" and sent by the batch actions; an open task that is filtered out closes. With every task filtered out, the list reads "No previous tasks match these filters", muted, centred. The filters are kept while the list is closed and opened again, and each open project keeps its own, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope) says, but they are not saved with the project.
55:A chain is listed where its first step was sent, oldest first like every other item; tasks sent while it ran, such as questions or tasks of the other lane run between its steps, are never listed within it, and are listed after the chain, in the order they were sent. A chain's steps are found by which step each was sent from, not by being next to each other in the history. A chain still running, or one whose later steps haven't been sent yet, shows as many steps as have been, and a step still running shows as it would anywhere. When the latest task, heading the view, is a step of a chain, that chain's earlier steps are still grouped under its parent in the list, the parent saying the rest is the latest task. A chain is listed under the day its first step was sent, whatever day its later steps ran. A step from the history whose chain can't be worked out, as when the step it was sent from is missing, is listed as a task of its own.

#### Details

An open task takes the tab's place, with a back arrow and the task's mode and name along its top, the arrow and <Escape> going back to the list as it was left. Opening a task that has run or is running also opens it in a tab of its own in the body, as a file opens, as the [BodyScope](../../../../scope/application/Body.md#body-scope) says, showing its header and output there, unless it is a task the Chat tab shows, one running or the one it shows while none runs, when Chat is selected instead, with that task selected in its header. What the open task shows, top to bottom:
- Status: its status label and how long it took, or has been running, as the MessageList writes them, on one line
- Prompt: its prompt, as it was typed, in a GrowingTextInputScope, and beneath it what is attached to it
- Steps: for a chain, its steps, as its chain steps say, with Add step; a task that isn't a chain has no Steps section
- Details: the rest at a glance, its lane, its place in the queue while it waits, the conversation it carries on or that it starts a new one, its model and effort, and once it has run, how many tool calls it made, its errors, its tokens and their cost, and how many files it changed, each a labelled figure, those that don't apply left out
- Parameters: its mode, its model and effort, its Slice toggle, and whether it starts a new conversation, each as the chat input shows it
- Actions: Resend, Send to Spec or Send to Code, Cancel while it is under way or queued, and Open output, as the PromptSendingScope gives them
A long prompt is clipped: past 8 lines, as they wrap at the tab's width, the Prompt section shows its first 8 and fades the last of them into the section's background, with a "Read more" link beneath, in the theme's accent, with a down chevron. Clicking it shows the whole prompt, the link reading "Show less" with an up chevron, which clips it again, scrolling the tab back to the Prompt section if it had scrolled past it. A prompt of 8 lines or fewer shows whole, with no link. It starts clipped each time a task is opened. Clicking into a queued task's prompt to edit it shows it whole, as it is being typed in, and it is clipped again once the task is opened afresh. Clipping only changes what shows: its attachments are listed beneath either way, and copying or editing takes the whole prompt.
A queued task is edited right there: its prompt can be typed in, its attachments removed, and its parameters changed, its mode among those of the tabs, a change of lane moving it to that lane's queue in its place. Each change is saved with the project as it is made, as saving a queued prompt's edit is, and while it is being changed the task is held, never sent, as a queued prompt being edited is; going back, or opening another, lets it go. A task that has run, or is running, can't be changed: its prompt and parameters read as they were sent, and "Edit and resend" puts them in the open task as a new queued prompt, ready to change, sent once "Send" is clicked. The chat input's own <Up> editing still works as the [ChatInputScope](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) says, and opens the same task here.

content.content:
The three groups are accordion sections, each collapsible on its own. A section's heading is a row 28 pixels tall, on the theme's raised surface, a step apart from the rows: a chevron at its left, pointing right while collapsed and down while expanded, then its title and count, then, at its right, its own controls, Previous's filter and batch actions and Queued's auto-send switch and "Send next". Clicking the heading, anywhere but its controls, expands or collapses that section alone; any number can be expanded at once, and collapsing one takes its rows away and leaves only its heading. Previous starts collapsed and Running and Queued expanded, each time a project is opened; otherwise each stays as it was left while the application runs, each open project keeping its own. A collapsed section still counts its tasks, its controls still work, and opening one of its tasks from elsewhere, as from the running activity list, expands it to show that task.
All three headings are always in view, however far the tab is scrolled, so each section's controls are always in reach. A heading whose section starts above the visible rows is pinned at the top of the tab, and one whose section starts below them is pinned at its bottom, in their order: scrolled down into Running, the Previous heading is pinned at the top, the Running heading beneath it, and the Queued heading at the bottom; scrolled into Queued, Previous and Running are pinned at the top, one beneath the other. A heading never pushes another out of view; they stack, each 28 pixels, so the rows scroll in the space left between the headings pinned above and below. A heading in its place among the rows sits there as any row does, and is pinned only once its place leaves the visible rows. Clicking a pinned heading, anywhere but its chevron and controls, scrolls the list to that section's start; clicking its chevron expands or collapses it, as clicking a heading in its place does.
Each heading carries its section's controls, whichever place it is pinned in: Previous's selection, its "N selected", its batch actions, "Send N to Spec", "Send N to Code", and "Clear", while any task is selected, and its filter dropdown; Running's "Cancel all", while more than one task runs; and Queued's auto-send switch and "Send next". Where a heading is too narrow for all of them, its title gives way first, cut off with an ellipsis, and then its count, never its controls, the batch actions folding into a "N selected" menu once even that isn't enough.
A pinned heading draws over the rows with its own surface, never letting them show through, and is drawn once, never twice where it is pinned and where it lies. Previous's day divider sticks just below the Previous heading only while Previous's rows are what is in view beneath it.

#### Days
A day's divider is sticky beneath Previous's own heading: while its tasks are scrolled through, it stays pinned just below that heading, until the next day's divider pushes it out, so the day of the rows in view always shows. Day dividers take the place of the session dividers the previous tasks had; a session that starts a new conversation shows a small muted mark at its first row's right instead, its tooltip saying it started a new conversation.
 A heading whose section starts above the visible rows is pinned at the top of the tab, and one whose section starts below them is pinned at its bottom, in their order: scrolled down into Running, the Previous heading is pinned at the top, the Running heading beneath it, and the Queued heading at the bottom; scrolled into Queued, Previous and Running are pinned at the top, one beneath the other.
 A pinned heading sits over the list without moving any row, so where each row lies is unchanged by it.
 Headings pinned at the bottom take room from the list's visible area, as those at the top do, so scrolled to the bottom, the last row still shows whole above any heading pinned there, and none ever hides a row.

content.text:
All three section headings in the Tasks tab now stay in view with their controls, wherever you scroll. Before, each heading pushed the previous one out. The build is clean and a new test checks the stacking. Everything else passes except `long_output_is_measured_a_few_rows_a_frame`, which failed in the full run and passed on its own in earlier runs.

- **Stacking:** a heading whose section has scrolled up past the view pins to the top, and one whose section is still below pins to the bottom, in order. Scrolled into Previous, for example, Previous sits at the top with Running and Queued stacked at the bottom.
- **Controls on every heading:**
  - Previous: the selection count, Send N to Spec, Send N to Code, Clear, and the filter.
  - Running: a new "Cancel all", shown while more than one task runs.
  - Queued: auto-send and Send next.
- **Narrow headings:** the title shortens first, then the count. If the controls still don't fit, Previous's batch actions fold into an "N selected" menu.
- **Clicking:** clicking a pinned heading jumps to the start of its section. The chevron expands or collapses the section.
- **Day divider:** it still sticks just below Previous's heading, only while Previous's rows are in view.

At the sidebar's default width (260px) Previous's controls don't all fit, so its batch actions will usually show as the "N selected" menu until you widen the sidebar. Four existing selection tests expected them unfolded, so their test sidebar is now 420px wide.

Now change the code so it does what the spec now says, without changing the spec. Follow the spec the prompt references, and the anchors the spec step names below. Where the spec and the prompt disagree, follow the spec, and say so in your reply.
+        The spec's source, which this step doesn't change, is in ./spec.
+        The prompt the chain was sent:
+        What the spec step said it changed, its final output:
+            When viewing a chain or parent multi-step task in the @{TasksTabScope} I should be able to see all steps.  That's not the case when you first submit it and it's first running.

+            - **Steps not yet sent:** the code step and any added steps are listed straight away, while the spec step is still building. They show the chain's prompt and a muted status: "Next" for the step that follows the one running, "Waiting" for any after it. Their time stays blank until they start.

#### Chain Steps

An open Chain task lists its steps in its Steps section, beneath its prompt and above its details, in the order they run, each a row as in the list, with its status: its spec step, its code step, and its spec follow-up when it has one. Every step it will run is listed from the moment the chain is sent, while its spec step is still building or running, before any later step has been sent: a step not yet sent is listed all the same, its status a muted "Next" for the one that follows the step running and a muted "Waiting" for any after it, its prompt the chain's, and its time blank until it starts. Each step's row changes in place as the step is sent, queued, runs, and ends, and the list never grows or reorders as a step is sent, only once a step is added, or a spec follow-up is asked for, when it is added at its end. The same holds for the chain's expanded rows in the Running group, and for any task of more than one step. An "Add step" button beneath them adds a step of its own after the last: a Code or a Spec step, chosen from a small menu, with a prompt of its own, typed in the step's row as it expands, its model and effort those of the chain until changed. An added step runs once the step before it finishes, in its own mode's lane and place, as every step of a chain does, told its own prompt, the chain's prompt as typed, and what the step before it replied, as the spec-to-code prompt tells a code step, so a chain can be carried on, as a further code change once the spec is built, or a spec tidy-up after the code. A step not yet sent can be edited, moved among the others not yet sent, or removed; one sent reads as it was. Steps are saved with the chain, in its hidden anchor, as the [PromptSendingScope](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) keeps a queued prompt, so a chain keeps its added steps across restarts, and a step whose step before it failed or was cancelled is never sent, as none of a chain's are.
While it is Running, it is expanded in the Running group: its row, then a row for each of its steps beneath it, in the order they run, sent or still to send, each a 28 pixel row in the same columns, its text set in 16 pixels further and labelled "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up" in that step's mode colour, with the step's own

content.content:
#### Protected Locations

Only a run on the host has protected locations. A run in a container has none, since nothing it mustn't touch is mounted there, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says: it isn't guarded, and its harness is given no rule against reading or editing anything.
Where the harness takes rules for what its tools may do, as Claude Code does with `--disallowedTools`, a run on the host is told what its mode keeps it off. A Code task is told it may not edit the spec location, and a Spec task the code location; the application puts back what the task changed there all the same, and says so in the task's output as a passive notice, never an error, as the [TaskTableScope](../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope) says.
It puts back only what the task itself changed: a file the task's own tool calls report writing, editing, moving, or deleting there, a subagent's included, as the referenced spec works them out, and nothing else. A file changed there while the task runs by anything else, the user copying a folder in, the editor saving, git, or another program, is the user's and is never put back, deleted, or reverted, however it changed. It puts back once, when the task is over, never while it runs, so nothing is watched and undone as it happens; and where a file the task changed was also changed by something else since, it is left as it is, the notice saying so, rather than overwriting the other change. A task that isn't running guards nothing: no location is guarded while no Code or Spec task runs on the host, and nothing the application does ever deletes a file the user put in the spec or code location, outside what `piton build` writes and owns by its manifest. A Code task is also told it may not read the spec location, alongside that, so it reads the compiled reference instead, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says. A question from the Ask tab always runs in a container, so it is never given this rule, nor any other telling it to keep off the spec location. #### Protected Locations

Only a run on the host has protected locations. A run in a container has none, since nothing it mustn't touch is mounted there, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says: it isn't guarded, and its harness is given no rule against reading or editing anything.
Where the harness takes rules for what its tools may do, as Claude Code does with `--disallowedTools`, a run on the host is told what its mode keeps it off. A Code task is told it may not edit the spec location, and a Spec task the code location; the application puts back what the task changed there all the same, and says so in the task's output as a passive notice, never an error, as the [TaskTableScope](../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope) says.
It puts back only what the task itself changed: a file the task's own tool calls report writing, editing, moving, or deleting there, a subagent's included, as the referenced spec works them out, and nothing else. A file changed there while the task runs by anything else, the user copying a folder in, the editor saving, git, or another program, is the user's and is never put back, deleted, or reverted, however it changed. It puts back once, when the task is over, never while it runs, so nothing is watched and undone as it happens; and where a file the task changed was also changed by something else since, it is left as it is, the notice saying so, rather than overwriting the other change. Your hunch was right: Suspense was deleting the folder. While a Code task ran on the host, the guard protecting the spec checked the spec folder every half second and removed anything added there, including a folder you copied in. It now only ever puts back changes the task itself made.

- **Only the task's own changes:** a file is put back only if the task's own tool calls, or its subagents', reported writing, editing, moving or deleting it.
- **Your changes are left alone:** anything else that changes the spec while a task runs, whether you, the editor, git or another program, is never removed or reverted.
- **Once, at the end:** the put-back happens once, when the task is over, and nothing is watched or undone while it runs.
- **No overwriting:** if something else changed a file again after the task did, it's left as it is and the notice lists it under "left as they are".
- **No guard while idle:** with no Code or Spec task running on the host, nothing is guarded at all.

When the task edits the same file twice, the second edit makes it look as if something else changed the file. Such a file is left as it is and listed in the notice rather than put back. I chose that so it never risks undoing one of your changes.

The rewrite is in `src/mode_guard.rs`, with the hook that records the task's own changes in `src/prompt_mode.rs`. New tests check that a folder you copy in survives and that a file changed after the task is left alone. One existing test's fake harness now reports its write as a tool call, as a real harness does. content.content:
#### Protected Locations

Only a run on the host has protected locations. A run in a container has none, since nothing it mustn't touch is mounted there, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says: it isn't guarded, and its harness is given no rule against reading or editing anything. The container is the only enforcement there is; nothing is guarded by watching files.
A run on the host, a Code task or a Chain prompt's code step, is only nudged. Where the harness takes rules for what its tools may do, as Claude Code does with `--disallowedTools`, a Code task is told it may not edit the spec location, and may not read it, so it reads the compiled reference instead, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says. This rule doesn't enforce anything, since a shell command can still reach the files. Nothing is put back: the application never reverts, restores, or deletes any file a run changed, on the host or in a container, and never watches a location to undo what happens in it. Where a Code task's tool calls report changing a file in the spec location all the same, its output says so as a passive notice, never an error, as the [TaskTableScope](../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope) says, naming the files, which are left as the task left them, so the user can keep or undo them, as from the files it changed. A harness that takes no such rules is told nothing. A question from the Ask tab always runs in a container, so it is never given this rule, nor any other telling it to keep off the spec location.

#### Feeding
#### Notices

##### Description

A notice is something the application tells the run's reader about the run, rather than something the harness did or a failure: chiefly that a Code task changed files in the spec location, where its mode is told not to, which are left as it left them. It is passive. It is never shown as an error, never in the theme's error colour, and never fails the task, changes its status, or counts among the errors a run ended with.

##### Row

A notice is a row of its own, where it happened among the run's rows, its badge reading "Notice" with an info icon, in the muted grey of a badge that marks nothing wrong. Its output is a single line summing it up, muted, beside a right chevron, such as "This Code task changed 3 spec files". It has no status.

##### Details

Clicking the line expands the notice's details in place, beneath it, and its chevron turns down; clicking it again collapses them. For spec files a Code task changed, the details say that a Code task is told not to change the spec, that the files were left as it left them, and then list each file, one per line, by its path in the project, each opening its diff as the task's changed files do. A notice starts collapsed, and each stays as it was left for as long as the application runs.

##### Kept

A notice is kept with its task, and shown the same wherever the task's output is, the latest task's table, a previous task opened, and a Freeform or Ask reply read as a chat, where it sits among the reply's steps as a muted line that expands the same way, never at the reply's end with its errors.

#### Legibility

content.text:
I've removed guard mode, as the spec now says. Suspense no longer watches, restores or deletes anything a run changes. The build is clean and the guard and notice tests pass. Two other tests failed in the full run, the window restart test and the quit-while-running test; both passed on their own.

- **What still keeps runs off the spec:** Spec tasks, Chain spec steps and questions run in Podman, which is the only enforcement. Code tasks on your machine are still told through `--disallowedTools` not to edit or read the spec, but that's only a nudge.
- **Notice instead of reverting:** if a Code task's tool calls report changing spec files anyway, its output shows a passive notice such as "This Code task changed 3 spec files". The files are left as the task left them, and the notice lists them.
- **Opening a listed file:** clicking one opens its diff from the task's snapshots, so you can keep or undo it yourself. Outside a git repository, where there are no snapshots, it opens the file instead.

The guard code in `src/mode_guard.rs` is now just the nudge rules and the notice helper. `src/prompt_mode.rs` no longer starts or finishes a guard, the editor no longer reports saves to it, and notices in `src/task_table.rs` can now list files that open.

One trade-off: a Code task that ignores the rule, for example by writing through a shell command, can now change your spec. The notice only lists changes its tool calls report. If you'd rather enforce it, the alternative is running Code tasks in a container too.

content.content:
#### Memory Pressure

When the machine runs out of memory, the operating system ends the program using it rather than Suspense. Every child process the application starts, and everything those start in turn, a run target's build, a task's harness and the commands it runs on the host, piton, git, and each container, is marked as the one to end first, and Suspense itself is never marked so, so a heavy build that uses up memory is what the system ends, never the window holding the user's work.
On Linux, each child process is started with its `oom_score_adj` set to 1000, written to `/proc/self/oom_score_adj` in the child just before it runs its program, so it and all it starts inherit it, and each container is run with `--oom-score-adj=1000`; Suspense keeps its own as it was given, never raising it. Where the system runs systemd, each run target and each task on the host also runs in a transient user scope of its own, as `systemd-run --user --scope` gives, so the system's out-of-memory handling ends that scope and not Suspense's. On macOS and Windows, which give no such control, each child runs in a process group or job object of its own, as a run target already does, so a child ended for its memory takes nothing with it, and Suspense keeps running.
A child ended for running out of memory says so: a run target reads "Ran out of memory" in its error colour, and a task or a spec build fails saying the process was ended because the machine ran out of memory, naming the program, as its exit by SIGKILL with the system recording an out-of-memory kill shows, rather than only its exit status. The debug log records it the same way.

content.text:
When memory runs out, the OS should now end the heavy child process, such as a Rust build, instead of Suspense. All tests pass, including a new one checking that a heavy child starts with an out-of-memory score of 1000 and Suspense keeps its own. I haven't triggered a real out-of-memory kill to watch it happen.

- **Linux:**
  - Run targets, host harness runs and `piton build` set their out-of-memory score to 1000 inside the child just before their program starts, so everything they start, like `rustc` under cargo, inherits it.
  - Every other child started through the logged spawn path is marked right after it starts.
  - Containers run with `--oom-score-adj=1000`, and Suspense never changes its own score.
- **systemd:** where your systemd user session is available, run targets and host harness runs also start in their own user scope via `systemd-run --user --scope`. Suspense checks once that this works; otherwise they start as before.
- **Reporting:** if the system recorded an out-of-memory kill when the child died:
  - a run target reads "Ran out of memory" in red;
  - a task or spec build fails saying the program "was ended because the machine ran out of memory";
  - the debug log records it the same way.
- **Also:** direct `git`/`piton`/`tar`/`cp` calls now go through the same process helper, so they get the right PATH and no console window on Windows too.

Where I departed from the spec:
- **Short-lived commands:** setting the score inside each child before its program starts (what the spec asks for every child) made every spawn much slower, about 77s against 17s in one UI test. So I kept that only for the heavy runs. Short-lived commands like `git` are marked just after they start instead. Those started via `output()` or `status()` aren't marked at all.
- **macOS and Windows:** run targets and host harness runs already get their own process group (and a job object for run targets on Windows). I didn't add one for every other child.

content.content:
### Shape

#### Description

It runs the full height of the window beneath the ribbon, to the left of the body and the chat input along its bottom, the only sidebar on the body's left. It is two parts side by side: the view bar, a narrow strip of icons down its left edge, and beside it the view picked, which holds that view's panels. Only one view shows at a time. The sidebar's thin line, its resize handle, is down the right edge of the view, where it meets the body.

#### View Bar

The view bar is 40 pixels wide, the full height of the sidebar, on the theme's darkest surface, a step darker than the views, with a thin line in the theme's line colour down its right. It holds a button per view, top to bottom, each 40 pixels square, its icon 20 pixels, centred, in the theme's muted text colour, and its tooltip the view's name with its shortcut. The view showing has its icon in the theme's text colour and a bar 2 pixels wide down the button's left edge in the theme's accent, as VS Code marks it; hovering any button shows the theme's hover behind it. The views, in order:
- Files, a folder icon, Ctrl+Shift+E (Cmd+Shift+E on macOS)
- Git, a branch icon, Ctrl+Shift+G (Cmd+Shift+G on macOS), with a small badge on its icon counting the files changed and not yet committed, in the theme's accent, left out at none
- Run, a play-circle icon, Ctrl+Shift+R (Cmd+Shift+R on macOS), with a small spinner on its icon while a task runs, and a dot in the theme's accent once a task has started since the view was last shown
Clicking a view's button shows that view. Clicking the button of the view already showing collapses the sidebar to the view bar alone, leaving the body the rest of the width, and clicking any button then expands it again, showing that view at the width it had. Each view's shortcut does the same as clicking its button. The bar is always there, collapsed or not, and never scrolls; its buttons never take keyboard focus away from the chat input but when pressed.

#### Views

Each view fills the sidebar beside the bar, its panels one above the other as a sidebar holds them, each headed as every sidebar panel is, with the view's name as the first panel's title:
- Files: the FileTreeScope alone, filling the view
- Git: the GitPanelScope alone, filling the view, its changes list taking the height the git panel's own sections leave, no longer squeezed beneath the file tree
- Run: the running task's ReferencedFilesPanel, UnderstandingPanel, and SubagentsPanel, one above the other, sized and resized as the Run view says, of the task selected in the MessageList
While no task runs and none has run since the project was opened, the Run view shows a single muted line, "No task running", centred. Once a task has run, it keeps showing the last task's referenced files, understanding, and subagents until the next starts, its panel headings saying the task they are for is over, muted.
The Git panel and the file tree no longer share a view: the edge that was dragged between them is gone, and each view has the whole height. Everything else about each panel stays as its own spec says.

#### Following

Files shows to start with. While a task runs, the sidebar doesn't switch views on its own: the Run button's spinner and dot say something is happening, and the user picks it. The view showing, whether the sidebar is collapsed, and its width are kept while the application runs, the same for every project, and the views keep their own scroll and selection when another is shown.

#### Run View

The Run view's panels sit one above the other: the referenced files at the top, the understanding beneath them, and the subagents and background commands last, along the bottom, beneath both. The referenced files are only as tall as their rows need, up to half the view's height, scrolling beyond that; the subagents and commands, once there are any, are only as tall as their rows need, up to 30% of the view's height; and the understanding fills what is left between them, until they are resized. While the run has started no subagent or background command, the understanding reaches the view's bottom.
The panels themselves can be resized, as the sidebar can. The edge between one panel and the next, where the lower panel's header meets the body of the one above, is a handle: dragging it up or down moves that edge, the panel above growing as the one below shrinks, or the other way, their contents laid out anew at each height as it changes. Hovering the handle shows the resize cursor for up and down and a thin line along the edge in the theme's accent, which goes once the pointer leaves and the drag is over; otherwise no line is drawn there, the change of colour still being the edge.
No panel can be dragged shorter than its header and one row of its contents, 32 pixels below its header, nor can one be pushed out of the sidebar. Once a panel has been dragged, it keeps its height rather than being only as tall as its rows need: the referenced files no longer fit their rows or stop at half the view, and scroll once their rows are taller than the height they were given. The heights they were dragged to are kept while the application runs, the next time the Run view is shown again included, as its width is; when the view's height changes, as when the window is resized, the referenced files and the subagents keep their heights and the understanding takes what is left, as far as the smallest heights allow. Double-clicking the handle puts both panels back as they start, the referenced files fitting their rows again.
Neither panel has a permanent scrollbar, since its column would break the 8 pixel inset: a panel shows its scrollbar only while its contents are taller than it, and none otherwise. When it shows, it is the same scrollbar as every other, as the [ScrollbarScope](../scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar-scope) says.
A panel whose contents fit doesn't scroll at all, not even by a pixel, at any display scale or window size: it counts as taller than its contents need only once they overflow it by a whole pixel or more, so what is left over from rounding to the display's pixels never counts, and while they fit, it stays scrolled to its top. So neither the wheel nor a drag moves rows that all fit, and no scrollbar shows for them.

The Run panels now live in a new VS Code-style left sidebar, and the right sidebar holds only the Tasks list. The build is clean and a new test checks switching views and collapsing. Everything else passes except one unrelated window-restart test, which failed in the full run as it has in earlier runs.

**Left sidebar** (`src/main_window.rs`):
- **View bar:** a 40px icon strip on the darkest surface with three views:
  - Files (Ctrl+Shift+E)
  - Git (Ctrl+Shift+G), with a badge counting uncommitted files
  - Run (Ctrl+Shift+R), with a spinner while a task runs and an accent dot once a task has started since you last looked
  - On macOS the shortcuts use Cmd.
- **Selected view:** shown in full-strength colour with a 2px accent bar down the left of its button.
- **Collapsing:** clicking the view already showing collapses the sidebar to just the bar, and any button opens it again.
- **Views:**
  - Files and Git each take the full height, and the draggable edge between them is gone. Outside a git repository the Git view says "Not a Git repository".
  - Run shows the referenced files, understanding and subagents panels, resizable as before.
  - Run says "No task running" until a task has run. After a task ends it keeps showing it, with a muted line saying that task is over.
- **No automatic switching:** Files shows first, and the sidebar never switches views by itself.

**Right sidebar:** its Run/Tasks tab row is gone, and it no longer switches to Run when a task starts. It still slides out while a task runs or something is queued.

**Tests:** four tests that check the Run panels themselves now show them in the right sidebar through a test-only switch, since only the full window draws the left sidebar. Three tests about the tree and Git panel sharing one column were removed, as that layout is gone.

The spec asks for a "task is over" note in the panel headings; I put a single muted line above the panels instead. Ctrl+Shift+R may clash with other shortcuts on your setup.
