#### Sent Prompt

##### Description

A task's header is one slim line, 32 pixels tall, across the view's full width, and nothing more: it never shows the prompt, the compiled markdown, or the hidden anchor's name. From left to right, 8 pixels in, come a bar 4 pixels wide with corners rounded 2 pixels, inset 6 pixels from the header's top and bottom, in the colour of the mode the task was sent in, as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it, the step's mode for a step of a chain, telling where it came from; its status, a spinner while it is under way and its status label, with its elapsed time beside it, as the status says; then its summary, in small text, cut off with an ellipsis; then, at its right, its buttons. The header is on the tab bar's background, faintly tinted the mode's colour, a sixth of its strength, never the stronger tint it had.

##### Summary

The summary is a short line saying what the task is for: its title, the words its hidden anchor was named from, as "Chat titles from the agent", or, where it was named at random or not yet named, the first line of its prompt as typed. For a step of a chain, the step's label, "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up", comes first, in its mode's colour, then the chain's summary. Hovering the summary shows the prompt's first lines as its tooltip.

##### Buttons

At the header's right, two small ghost buttons, 24 pixels tall, 4 pixels apart. "Stop", with a stop icon, while the task is building, compiling, or running, cancels it as Cancel does, as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says, and is gone once it is over. "View all", with a list icon, opens the task in the right sidebar's Tasks tab, as the [TasksTabScope](../../../ui/components/right-sidebar/tasks/index.md#tasks-tab-scope) opens a task, where its prompt, steps, details, parameters, and the rest of its actions are, opening the sidebar first if it is closed. The header has no Resend, no Send to Spec or Send to Code, and no other button: those are in the Tasks tab.

#### Status
#### Backgrounds

##### Description

The header for the latest task shows where it came from by its mode's colour, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope): a bar in that colour at its left and a faint tint of it behind it, as its sent prompt says, never a strong fill. A task from the history that doesn't say which mode it was sent in has no bar and keeps the tab bar's colour.
Each task in the previous tasks list hints at the mode it was sent in: its heading's background is a faint tint of that mode's colour, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope), red for Code, purple for Chain, blue for Spec, green for Ask, and grey for Freeform, far fainter than the latest task's header, so the list reads as a column of the list's own background with each task only touched by its colour. A task whose mode isn't known, as one from the history that doesn't say, keeps the list's background untinted. Its status label, prompt, checkbox, and buttons stay readable over the tint, in light and dark mode, and its hover and open states still show over it. An open task's prompt and output beneath its heading are not tinted.

#### Referenced Spec
#### Header

The latest task heads the view whether or not the harness is working. It is always the most recent task still active: of the tasks under way, building, compiling, or running, in either lane, the one sent most recently. Only while no task is under way is it the task that finished most recently, or, before any has finished, the one sent most recently. A finished task never heads the view while another is under way: when it finishes while a task in the other lane still runs, that task heads the view in its place at once, and the task that finished goes among the previous tasks. So with two Chain tasks sent one after the other, once both their spec steps have finished, the first chain's code step heads the view while it runs, not the second chain's finished spec step, and the second chain's code step heads it in turn once it is sent. A task still running in the other lane that is not the latest is among the previous tasks, shown running there, as any previous task is. Whichever task heads the view, its header and output show as they do for a task just sent, and the previous tasks, their row's count, and the chain grouping follow it. The header shows a single slim line, as the [MessageList](./message-list/index.md#message-list)'s sent prompt says: a bar in its mode's colour, its status and time, its summary, and a Stop and a View all button, never the prompt itself or the compiled markdown, which are seen in the Tasks tab. Messages sent to it while it runs are shown in its output.

#### Raw Prompt

content.content:
#### Raw Prompt

Beside the latest task's Resend button, a small ghost button with a code icon, whose tooltip says "View the raw prompt", opens a modal showing exactly what the harness was given for the task, once it has been sent: nothing rendered, nothing hidden. Clicking it never opens or closes anything else in the header. Until the task has compiled, it is disabled, its tooltip reading "No prompt sent yet". Only the latest task's header has it; previous tasks and questions don't.
The modal is titled "Raw prompt", with the task's mode, its hidden anchor's name, and the harness it was sent to beneath the title, or "Harness not recorded" for a task saved before the harness was. The anchor's name is shown for a Freeform task too, though its header hides it. It shows two sections, each headed and each with a Copy button that copies that section's whole text, disabled while the section has none to copy:
- System prompt: the system prompt as the harness received it, with
  every placeholder filled in and every injected prompt in its place,

- `attachments/`: every file other than an image attached to a task or question, saved when it is sent or queued, under its own name, in a folder named by the second it was saved and a short hash of its content, so the same file attached twice is saved once, as the @{ChatInputScope} says
- [A conversation left for a new one is never carried on again](.claude/reference/scope/harness-integration/index.md#context)
- [A task's history record sits in .suspense/history/, named by second and anchor name](.claude/reference/scope/project-data/index.md#contents)
- [Questions are saved in asks/ the same way as tasks](.claude/reference/scope/project-data/index.md#contents)

+- [Sessions never expire: cleanup off, copied beside each record after a run, restored before resuming; fresh only with no copy or when left](.claude/reference/scope/harness-integration/index.md#context)
+        Ask mode shouldn't split the @{BodyScope} it should fully replace it just like any other mode.
+        We're working on both the spec and the code, as a chain. This first step changes the spec only, located in ./spec; the code is changed in the next step.

+        Write the spec so it describes the application as it should be once the prompt is met, and constrains the code. Once you finish, the spec will be built and the same prompt sent to a coding agent, with your reply, to change the code to match it; so end your reply by saying what you changed in the spec and which anchors the code should follow.

+        When the work is about Suspense, its modes, its prompts, or its questions, or you are to write a prompt or a question for the user, first read .suspense/suspense-fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Suspense works.
+        Before creating or editing any .pi file, read .suspense/fluency.md once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.

+        Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton check` and fix every error it reports, then run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under .claude/reference, not by reading the source again. Never finish with a spec that `piton check` or `piton build` reports errors in.

+        Once you have read what the change depends on, and before your first change, write the constraints this task must meet to ${UNDERSTANDING_FILE}, once. Rewrite it only when a constraint in it turns out to be wrong, never after each page you read. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.
+        End with a reply of a few sentences saying what changed, or for a question, the answer, not a recap of the work or of what you read.

The task header at the top of the Chat tab is now one slim 32px line. The build is clean. In the full test run three tests failed, a server-output one, a window-restart one and a long-output layout one; each passed when run on its own, and none is about the header. content.content:
## Images

Images attached to a prompt, as the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) says, are given to the harness as it takes them: to Claude Code as image content blocks, base64-encoded with their media type, in the same stream-json user message as the prompt's text, after it; to Codex with an `--image` argument per image; and to OpenCode with a `--file` argument per image. A message fed to a running Claude Code task carries its images the same way, and a Claude Code run that isn't fed more but has images is given its prompt as a stream-json message too, so the images can go with it. Codex's options end with `--` before the prompt when it is given images. Questions take images as tasks do.

## Context

The harness keeps its context between requests instead of starting fresh each time. Each lane of the [PromptSendingScope](../prompt-mode/sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) carries on a conversation of its own, so nothing a task of one lane read reaches a task of the other: the spec lane's, carried on by Spec tasks and a Chain prompt's spec steps, and the code lane's, carried on by Code tasks, a Chain prompt's code step, and Freeform tasks. Each task sent carries on its own lane's, and since a lane runs one task at a time, two tasks never carry on the same conversation at once. A Chain prompt's steps hand on to each other as text, the prompt and what the step before replied, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says, so the handoff crosses lanes whatever each lane's conversation holds. When the project is opened, each lane carries on the latest conversation among its own tasks in the history, a Chain task by the lane of the step it was.
The spec lane and the questions always run in a container, and the code lane always on the host, so each conversation is only ever carried on where it began. A run in a container keeps its conversation's sessions in the project, in its own folder of `.suspense/sessions/`, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says, so it carries on across runs, restarts of the application, and moves of the project; a run on the host keeps them where the harness keeps them on the host.
Questions from the Ask tab share a separate conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they carry on the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question asked while another is running carries on a copy of that conversation, so questions running at the same time never write over each other. A conversation is only carried on in the project it began in, each open project keeping its own tasks' and questions' conversations while it is in the background. A spec lane or questions conversation from before its sessions were kept in the project, whose session the project's sessions folder doesn't hold, is still tried, and when the harness has no such session, the request is sent again at once as a new conversation, as below.
A request whose conversation can't be carried on, because the harness says it has no such session, as Claude Code's "No conversation found", or because it was begun elsewhere, is never failed for it. Its session is first put back from the project's copy, as above, and the request carried on with it; only where there is no copy, or it still can't be carried on, is it never retried on the same conversation: it is sent again at once as a new conversation, the same prompt, with no context, and the conversation it couldn't carry on is not tried again by any later request, the project's history included. A question sent again so is recorded and shown as starting a new conversation, as the [AskConversationScope](../prompt-mode/ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation-scope) marks one. Each run applies its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a conversation begun in a different mode. The palette's file search always starts fresh.
A conversation the application carries on never expires on its own. Every Claude Code run the application starts, on the host or in a container, is run with its transcript cleanup turned off, as its `cleanupPeriodDays` setting given so that no session is ever old enough to be deleted, passed with the run rather than written to the user's own settings, so Claude Code never deletes a session for its age.
When a run is over, however it ended, the application copies the harness's session for its conversation, its transcript and whatever the harness needs to resume it, into the project's data, beside the run's history record, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, replacing the copy an earlier run of the same conversation left. Before carrying on a conversation whose session the harness no longer has, as when it was cleaned up, the machine changed, or the session was kept on the host and the harness's own folder was cleared, it puts the latest copy back where the harness looks for it, under the same session id, so the conversation carries on with its context rather than starting a new one. Only where no copy of it exists, or it can't be put back, is the request sent again as a new conversation, as below, and a conversation the user left for a new one is never restored.
Codex and OpenCode sessions are kept and restored the same way, wherever each harness keeps them: Codex's under its sessions folder, and OpenCode's in its data directory, each copied after a run and put back before one that needs it. A run in a container restores into the conversation's sessions folder it mounts; a run on the host into the harness's own folder on the host.
A conversation can be left for a new one, from the chat input's New conversation button, as the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) says, which leaves the conversation of the lane it is used for: the next request in it starts a new conversation with no context, and the one left is not carried on again, not by a run of it still going, nor by the project's history. Leaving it is kept with the project, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, so a project opened after a lane's or the questions' conversation was left starts a new one there too, rather than carrying on the latest conversation in its history, until a run after the reset begins one of its own. How much context a conversation holds is known from what the harness reports with each reply: everything the model was given, cached or not, and what it wrote, as of its latest reply; replies of subagents don't count.

content.text:
A conversation's session is now kept in the project and put back when the harness has lost it, so conversations no longer expire. All tests pass, including a new one for copying a session and putting it back, but I haven't run a real conversation through the loss-and-restore path.

- **No cleanup:** every Claude Code run (tasks, questions, file search and the quick title/notes runs) gets `--settings {"cleanupPeriodDays":3650000}`, about 10,000 years. It's passed with the run and never written into your own Claude settings. Your installed Claude Code accepted the flag and ran normally; I didn't confirm it actually stops cleanup.
- **Copied after each run:** however a run ends, its conversation's session is copied into a `.session` folder beside the run's history record, for tasks and questions alike. It replaces what an earlier copy in that folder held.
- **Restored before resuming:** before carrying on a conversation, the harness is checked for its session. If it's gone, the newest `.session` copy holding that session id is put back where the harness looks, and the debug log says whether that worked.
- **Starting afresh:** only if there's no copy, or the harness still can't find it, does the existing "no conversation found → start a new one" path take over. A conversation you left for a new one is never resumed, so it's never restored.
- **Where sessions are found:** container runs use the sessions folder they mount, and host runs use the harness's own folder.
  - **Claude Code:** the transcript and its subfolder, under the folder for the working directory.
  - **Codex and OpenCode:** any file named by the session id under their sessions or storage folder.

The work is in a new `src/session_keep.rs`, hooked into `src/harness.rs` and `src/prompt_mode.rs`. This follows the spec, which matches your prompt.

Two limitations:
- **Another machine:** a host Claude Code session restored there goes under the current project path's folder. A copy taken from a container run is restored under the container's working folder.
- **Codex and OpenCode untested:** I matched their session files only by the id in the file name, and couldn't test either since neither is installed here.

13:The main window's body: the area to the right of the project sidebar, where the tasks sent to the harness, and the files opened in tabs beside them, are shown, and the chat input they are sent from.
18:The [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) lives within the body, along its bottom: its left edge against the project sidebar, and above it, beneath the body's tab bar, the selected tab's contents: the message list, or an open file. While a task runs, the [RightSidebarScope](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar-scope) runs the body's full height at its right, beside the tab bar, the selected tab's contents, and the chat input, and the chat input's right edge is against it: the chat input never runs beneath the right sidebar. While that sidebar isn't there, the chat input reaches the window's right edge.
23:Whenever something slides out or back along one of the body's edges, as the [RightSidebarScope](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar-scope) does, everything else in the body moves smoothly with it, frame by frame, rather than jumping once the slide is over: the tab bar, the selected tab's contents, the Ask conversation while it shows, and the chat input all keep their right edge against the sliding edge throughout, so they narrow or widen together, in step with it and with each other. None of them lags behind another, is left at its old width until the slide settles, or runs beneath what is sliding. Their contents are laid out anew at each width as it changes, text wrapping and rows reflowing as they go: the tab bar's tabs, the chat input's text and buttons, the message list's table, and an open file's editor. A slide that reverses partway moves them back from wher
31:- the hint shown in the message list's place before any task has been sent, or while no project is open, as the [PromptEditor](../prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor) and the [NoProjectStateScope](../no-project/index.md#no-project-state-scope) say
33:- a task view for each task opened in a tab of its own, as its task tabs say, shown beneath the tab bar while its tab is selected
34:- the [AskConversationScope](../prompt-mode/ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation-scope), in the Chat tab's place beneath the tab bar, while the chat input's Ask tab is selected
35:- the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope), along the bottom beneath whichever tab is selected, and beneath the Ask conversation too
36:- the [RightSidebarScope](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar-scope), at the right of all of these, the tab bar and the chat input included, while a task runs or is queued, or it is opened by hand
40:## Ask Mode
42:While the chat input's Ask tab is selected, the Ask conversation, as the [AskConversationScope](../prompt-mode/ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation-scope) says, takes the Chat tab's place in the body, filling all of it beneath the tab bar and above the chat input, as the message list fills it for every other mode: the body never splits, and nothing is shown beside the conversation. The Chat tab then reads "Ask" in Ask's colour. Selecting another mode's tab brings the message list back in its place, as it was left, and selecting Ask again brings the conversation back, scrolled where it was; the switch is at once, with nothing sliding. A file or task tab selected shows that file or task whatever mode is selected, and selecting Ask while one is shown selects the Chat tab, so the conversation is in view.
46:Along the top of the body runs a tab bar, in gpui-kit's default tab styling, across the width the message list takes: from the project sidebar to the right sidebar while a task runs, and to the window's right edge otherwise. Its first tab, Chat, shows the message list, and is always there: it can't be closed or moved. After it comes a tab for each open file and each task opened in a tab of its own, files and tasks together, in the order they were opened unless they have been dragged since, scrolling sideways once there are more than fit.
52:## Task Tabs
54:The Chat tab shows only the task the harness is working on now, and those running beside it, as the [MessageList](../prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list)'s header shows them, or, while none runs, the task that finished last, until the next is sent. It never shows any other task: a task opened from the right sidebar's Tasks tab, as the [TasksTabScope](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/tasks/index.md#tasks-tab-scope) says, or from anywhere else that opens a task, opens in a tab of its own in the body's tab bar, as a file does: a task not open yet gets a new tab just after the one selected, and is selected; opening one that already has a tab selects that tab; and opening the task Chat is showing selects Chat instead.
55:A task's tab is laid out as a file's is: a bar 2 pixels wide down its left in its mode's colour, its status, a spinner while it is under way, a tick, cross, or dash once it has ended, then its name, the first line of its prompt cut off with an ellipsis at 24 characters, then its close button. Hovering it shows its prompt's first lines and its mode as its tooltip. It can be dragged among the files' tabs, and closed as they are, closing it changing nothing about the task.
56:Beneath it, the task shows as it would at the head of the Chat tab, on its own: its header, with its status, time, compiled prompt, and buttons, then its output table, then the files it changed, scrolled to its top the first time it is shown, and as it was left after. A task still running shows its output as it comes, its table locked to the bottom while scrolled there, as the latest task's is, and carries on in its tab whether or not the tab is selected. Its tab stays open once it finishes. Opening a task in a tab doesn't select it in the Chat tab or change what Chat shows, and Chat's running tasks are never opened in tabs of their own unless asked for, a running task opened from the Tasks tab selecting it in Chat's header instead. Each open project keeps its own task tabs, as its file tabs are kept, and none is reopened when the project is opened again.
62:Closing a file's tab, with its close button or the editor's, closes the file, the editor first asking to discard any unsaved changes. Closing the selected tab selects the tab to its right, or, with none to its right, the one to its left, which is Chat once no file is left. Closing a tab that isn't selected leaves the selection as it is.

## Pausing

A running task can be paused and resumed. A Pause button, a small ghost button with a pause icon, whose tooltip says "Pause this task", sits beside Cancel wherever Cancel does, shown while the task is running. Pausing stops the harness's run, its process ended as cancelling ends it, and leaves the task in the history as "Paused": its output, its conversation, and the snapshot taken as it first started are kept, and nothing it changed is undone. A paused task is not under way: its lane is free, and its queue carries on with the next prompt, as after any task.
A paused task offers Resume, a small ghost button with a play icon, in place of Pause, wherever its actions are. Resume carries on the same task, never a new one: it is not saved in the history again and keeps its name. It carries on the task's own conversation, as the [HarnessIntegration](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says, with a message telling the harness that its run was interrupted, that any step it was in the middle of may not have finished, and that files may have changed since, so it checks what it needs before carrying on from where it left off rather than starting over. The message is the application's own, from the [ModeSystemPrompts](../mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts), not the user's, and it is not compiled as a prompt; the spec is not built again ahead of it. A resumed task takes its place in its lane's queue as a task sent at the time it was first

### Sent

it runs as soon as its lane is free, ahead of every prompt sent

after it was first sent.
While it is paused, its status reads "Paused", its time stops, and it is listed among the previous tasks, or, for a chain step, with its chain. Once resumed, its output carries on beneath what it had, a muted row marking where it was paused and resumed, its time counts on from where it stopped, counting only while it runs, and its changed files and their diffs span the whole task, from the snapshot taken when it first started to the one taken when it finally ends. It can be paused and resumed any number of times, and cancelled while paused, which ends it as Cancelled. A paused task whose conversation can no longer be carried on resumes as a new conversation, as the [HarnessIntegration](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says, told the task's prompt and its output so far.
A paused Chain step resumes as that step, and the chain carries on after it as ever, its next step sent once it finishes. While one of its steps is paused and none runs, the chain reads Paused.
A task also pauses this way, rather than failing, when it stops because the harness's usage limit was reached, as the harness says in its result or its errors: it reads "Paused" with a muted note saying the usage limit was reached and when it resets, if the harness says, and waits to be resumed by hand. Paused tasks are kept across restarts and can be resumed after one.

## Resuming

The resume prompt is the message given to a paused task when it is resumed, as the [PromptSending](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says, sent on its own as the next message of the task's conversation, never compiled as a prompt. Like the injected prompts, each project has its own, saved with its data in resume.md beside the templates, and edited in the [SettingsWindow](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window); with no file yet the project uses its default, which says:
Your previous run on this task was interrupted before it finished. Any step you were in the middle of, such as an edit, a command, or a build, may not have completed, and files may have changed since. Before carrying on, check the state of what you were working on: re-read the files you were changing and re-run any check you need. Then carry on from where you left off; don't start the task over or redo work that is already done.

## Saving

Each project has its own system template, instructions, and injected prompts, saved with its data, as the [ProjectData](../../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, a Markdown file each, system.md for the system template, code.md, combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md for the modes, and edited in the [SettingsWindow](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window). One with no file yet gives its default.

## Understanding File

Each Code, Chain, or Spec task has an understanding file: the short list of constraints the harness has taken from the spec for it, which the [LeftSidebar](../../../ui/components/left-sidebar/index.md#left-sidebar)'s Run view shows as it changes. It is saved beside the task's history record, with the same name and the extension `.understanding.md`, written by the harness itself. Nothing else writes it, and nothing is there until the harness writes it. Each constraint links to the compiled reference file it comes from, never to the spec's source.

## Defaults

The defaults are the prompts saved in this application's own repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, named as a project's are. They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made without them.
The system template's default says what the project is, where its code is and where its spec is, each on a paragraph of its own, so the one a run can't see goes, that each prompt starts with a <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it may change, and then SPEC_READING on a paragraph of its own. It holds no fluency.
The spec-reading prompt's default says:
Read the spec from its compiled reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

At the header's right, small ghost buttons, 24 pixels tall, 4 pixels apart. "Pause", with a pause icon, while the task is running, pauses it, and "Resume", with a play icon, in its place while it is paused, resumes it, as the [PromptSending](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says. "Stop", with a stop icon, while the task is building, compiling, running, or paused, cancels it as Cancel does, as the [PromptSending](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says, and is gone once it is over. "View all", with a list icon, opens the task in the right sidebar's Tasks tab, as the [TasksTab](../../../ui/components/right-sidebar/tasks/index.md#tasks-tab) opens a task, where its prompt, steps, details, parameters, and the rest of its actions are, opening the sidebar first if it is closed. The header has no Resend, no Send to Spec or Send to Code, and no other button: those are in the Tasks tab.

They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made without them.
The system template's default says what the project is, where its code is and where its spec is, each on a paragraph of its own, so the one a run can't see goes, that each prompt starts with a <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it may change, and then SPEC_READING on a paragraph of its own. It holds no fluency.
The spec-reading prompt's default says:
Read the spec from its compiled reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

At the header's right, small ghost buttons, 24 pixels tall, 4 pixels apart. "Pause", with a pause icon, while the task is running, pauses it, and "Resume", with a play icon, in its place while it is paused, resumes it, as the [PromptSending](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says. "Stop", with a stop icon, while the task is building, compiling, running, or paused, cancels it as Cancel does, as the [PromptSending](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says, and is gone once it is over. "View all", with a list icon, opens the task in the right sidebar's Tasks tab, as the [TasksTab](../../../ui/components/right-sidebar/tasks/index.md#tasks-tab) opens a task, where its prompt, steps, details, parameters, and the rest of its actions are, opening the sidebar first if it is closed. The header has no Resend, no Send to Spec or Send to Code, and no other button: those are in the Tasks tab.

1	//! Keeps a conversation's session from expiring, as the
2	//! HarnessIntegrationScope's context says: once a run is over, the harness's
3	//! session for its conversation is copied into the project's data, a
4	//! `.session` folder beside the run's history record; and before a
5	//! conversation is carried on whose session the harness no longer has, the
6	//! latest copy is put back where the harness looks for it, under the same
7	//! session id.
8	//!
9	//! A session is whatever the harness keeps under its sessions folder named
10	//! by the session's id: Claude Code's transcript `<id>.jsonl` and its folder
11	//! `<id>/`, beneath the folder of the run's working directory; Codex's
12	//! `rollout-…-<id>.jsonl` beneath its dated folders; and OpenCode's files
13	//! named by the id across its storage. Each is copied at its path from the
14	//! sessions folder, so it goes back to the same place.
15	
16	use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
17	
18	use crate::agent::Agent;
19	use crate::hidden_anchor::APP_DIR;
20	
21	/// How deep beneath a sessions folder a session's files are looked for.
22	const DEPTH: usize = 6;
23	
24	/// The settings every Claude Code run is given, so it never deletes a
25	/// session for its age: its transcript cleanup set further off than any
26	/// session will ever be old. Passed with the run, never written to the
27	/// user's own settings.
28	pub const CLAUDE_SETTINGS: &str = r#"{"cleanupPeriodDays":3650000}"#;
29	
30	/// Where `agent` keeps its sessions for a run: the conversation's sessions
31	/// folder it mounts, for a run in a container, or the harness's own folder
32	/// on the host.
33	pub fn sessions_root(agent: Agent, mounted: Option<&Path>) -> Option<PathBuf> {
34	    if let Some(mounted) = mounted {
35	        return Some(mounted.to_path_buf());
36	    }
37	    let home = dirs::home_dir()?;
38	    Some(home.join(match agent {
39	        Agent::Claude => ".claude/projects",
40	        Agent::Codex => ".codex/sessions",
41	        Agent::OpenCode => ".local/share/opencode/storage",
42	    }))
43	}
44	
45	/// The folder Claude Code keeps a working directory's transcripts in, named
46	/// by the directory with every character but letters and digits a dash.
47	fn claude_folder(cwd: &Path) -> String {
48	    cwd.to_string_lossy()
49	        .chars()
50	        .map(|c| if c.is_ascii_alphanumeric() { c } else { '-' })
51	        .collect()
52	}
53	
54	/// Where beneath `root` to look for a session of `agent` run in `cwd`:
55	/// Claude Code's folder for the directory, and the whole of the others'.
56	fn search_root(agent: Agent, root: &Path, cwd: &Path) -> PathBuf {
57	    match agent {
58	        Agent::Claude => root.join(claude_folder(cwd)),
59	        Agent::Codex | Agent::OpenCode => root.to_path_buf(),
60	    }
61	}
62	
63	/// Every file or folder beneath `dir` named by `id`, a folder taken whole.
64	fn named_by(dir: &Path, id: &str) -> Vec<PathBuf> {
65	    let mut found = Vec::new();
66	    let mut folders = vec![(dir.to_path_buf(), 0)];
67	    while let Some((folder, depth)) = folders.pop() {
68	        let Ok(entries) = std::fs::read_dir(&folder) else {
69	            continue;
70	        };
71	        for entry in entries.flatten() {
72	            let path = entry.path();
73	            let named = entry.file_name().to_string_lossy().contains(id);
74	            let is_dir = entry.file_type().is_ok_and(|kind| kind.is_dir());
75	            if named {
76	                found.push(path);
77	            } else if is_dir && depth < DEPTH {
78	                folders.push((path, depth + 1));
79	            }
80	        }
81	    }
82	    found
83	}
84	
85	/// Whether the harness still has the session `id`.
86	pub fn has(agent: Agent, root: &Path, cwd: &Path, id: &str) -> bool {
87	    !id.is_empty() && !named_by(&search_root(agent, root, cwd), id).is_empty()
88	}
89	
90	/// Copies the session `id`, as the harness left it beneath `root`, into
91	/// `kept`, the `.session` folder beside the run's history record, replacing
92	/// what an earlier copy there held. Nothing is copied where the harness has
93	/// no such session.
94	pub fn keep(agent: Agent, root: &Path, cwd: &Path, id: &str, kept: &Path) -> std::io::Result<()> {
95	    if id.is_empty() {
96	        return Ok(());
97	    }
98	    let searched = search_root(agent, root, cwd);
99	    let found = named_by(&searched, id);
100	    if found.is_empty() {
101	        return Ok(());
102	    }
103	    std::fs::remove_dir_all(kept).ok();
104	    for path in found {
105	        let relative = path.strip_prefix(&searched).unwrap_or(&path);
106	        copy(&path, &kept.join(relative))?;
107	    }
108	    Ok(())
109	}
110	
111	/// Puts the latest copy of the session `id` the project keeps back beneath
112	/// `root`, where the harness looks for it, at the same paths; whether one
113	/// was put back.
114	pub fn restore(agent: Agent, root: &Path, cwd: &Path, id: &str, project_dir: &Path) -> bool {
115	    let Some(kept) = latest_copy(project_dir, id) else {
116	        return false;
117	    };
118	    let searched = search_root(agent, root, cwd);
119	    let Ok(entries) = std::fs::read_dir(&kept) else {
120	        return false;
121	    };
122	    let mut restored = false;
123	    for entry in entries.flatten() {
124	        let to = searched.join(entry.file_name());
125	        if copy(&entry.path(), &to).is_ok() {
126	            restored = true;
127	        }
128	    }
129	    restored && has(agent, root, cwd, id)
130	}
131	
132	/// The latest `.session` folder the project's history holds for the
133	/// session `id`.
134	fn latest_copy(project_dir: &Path, id: &str) -> Option<PathBuf> {
135	    if id.is_empty() {
136	        return None;
137	    }
138	    let history = project_dir.join(APP_DIR).join("history");
139	    std::fs::read_dir(history)
140	        .ok()?
141	        .flatten()
142	        .map(|entry| entry.path())
143	        .filter(|path| path.extension().is_some_and(|ext| ext == "session") && path.is_dir())
144	        .filter(|path| !named_by(path, id).is_empty())
145	        .max_by_key(|path| {
146	            std::fs::metadata(path)
147	                .and_then(|meta| meta.modified())
148	                .ok()
149	        })
150	}
151	
152	/// Copies the file or folder `from` to `to`, its folders made as needed.
153	fn copy(from: &Path, to: &Path) -> std::io::Result<()> {
154	    if from.is_dir() {
155	        std::fs::create_dir_all(to)?;
156	        for entry in std::fs::read_dir(from)?.flatten() {
157	            copy(&entry.path(), &to.join(entry.file_name()))?;
158	        }
159	        Ok(())
160	    } else {
161	        if let Some(parent) = to.parent() {
162	            std::fs::create_dir_all(parent)?;
163	        }
164	        std::fs::copy(from, to).map(|_| ())
165	    }
166	}

content.text:
Pause and resume now work, and the build is clean. The new test passes, run both alone and with the full `prompt_mode` tests (three times in a row). The full suite still has failures that don't come from this change; details below.

**What it does:**
- **Pause:** a running task's header gets a Pause button beside Stop, and its Tasks tab details get one beside Cancel. Pausing stops the harness's run like cancelling does, but the task reads "Paused" in the warning colour. Its output, conversation and starting snapshot are all kept. Its lane is freed, so the queue moves on to the next prompt.
- **Resume:** a paused task shows Resume instead, and can still be cancelled. Resume carries on the same task, not a new one:
  - It sends `resume.md` (now in the project's system prompts, with the spec's default text) as the next message in the task's own conversation. Nothing is compiled and the spec isn't rebuilt.
  - Its output continues beneath "Resumed".
  - Its time doesn't count while paused.
  - Its changed files and diff run from the snapshot taken when it first started.
  - If its lane is busy, it waits and goes ahead of prompts queued after it was first sent.
- **Chains:** a paused chain step doesn't hand on to the next step. Once resumed and finished, the chain continues as normal. A chain with a paused step and nothing running reads "Paused".
- **Usage limit:** if the harness stops because its usage limit was reached, the task pauses instead of failing, with a note saying when the limit resets (when the harness has reported that).
- **Restarts:** the paused state and paused time are saved in the history record, so a paused task can still be resumed after a restart.

**Where I went beyond the prompt, following the spec:** if a paused task's conversation can't be carried on, it resumes in a new conversation. That message includes its original prompt and its output so far, followed by the resume prompt. I also added the resume prompt to the settings window's injected prompts.

**Test fixes:**
- The new test and the existing `cancelling` test both start real harness runs. They failed in the full suite because neither called `allow_parking()`, which the other harness-run tests use; I added it to both.
- A finished run now drops its event stream straight away.
- I updated the system-prompt and settings tests for the new Resume prompt.

**Still failing, not caused by this change:**
- 13 compile and completion tests in `hidden_anchor`, `piton_lsp`, `project_lsp`, `file_view` and `chat_input` fail because your uncommitted spec edits renamed `ApplicationScope` to `Application`.
- `long_output_is_measured_a_few_rows_a_frame` fails sometimes when run with the other tests. It also failed with my test switched off, and passes on its own.

# Scrollbar

## How To Build

A Scrollbar should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details. ## Theme

Drawn in the [Theme](../../theme/index.md#theme): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Pitch

A permanent scrollbar for any list that scrolls, laid out as a narrow column of its own beside the list rather than over it.

## Description

A narrow column along the right of the list, always shown, whether or not the list has anything to scroll. It is the list's only scrollbar: no scrollbar is laid over the list, or appears only while hovering or scrolling.

Every scrollbar is this one, wherever it is. It has no background of its own: the column takes the colour of the surface it sits on, so on the file tree it is the tree's colour, and on a panel's body the body's. Nothing in it is a colour of its own; its border, buttons, thumb, the thumb's ends, the arrows, and the lightening of the thumb and buttons are all white or black laid over that surface, so the scrollbar looks the same on any of them.
The strengths given here are dark mode's. Light mode takes the same steps, its raised parts lighter than the surface as in dark mode: the border, buttons, and thumb are white laid about a third of the way over the surface, the thumb's ends about a sixth, and the thumb and buttons lighten with white laid a fifth of the way while hovered and two fifths while pressed or dragged. Its arrows are darker than the buttons rather than lighter, black laid about a third of the way over them, since white would all but vanish on a light surface.

A square button at the top of the column scrolls the list up a little, and a square button at the bottom scrolls it down a little. The column is 18 pixels wide, and each button is 17 pixels tall, as wide as the column. A button is raised over the surface just as the thumb is, #222222 on #111111 in dark mode, with no bevel, border, or line of its own. It shows a small solid arrow, pointing up or down, 6 pixels wide and 4 tall, centred across it, 7 pixels from its top pointing up and from its bottom pointing down, drawn crisp on whole pixels rather than smoothed, in a faint grey, #4d4d4d on the button's #222222 in dark mode, white laid about a fifth of the way over the button. It lightens as the thumb does: a step while the pointer is over it, and another while pressed with the pointer still over it, across its whole face.

Between the buttons runs the track, from just beneath the top button to just above the bottom one. The track has no fill: it is the surface it sits on, #111111 on the file tree in dark mode. The whole column is bordered by a line a pixel wide down both its sides, in the buttons' and thumb's colour, #222222 in dark mode, so the border runs straight into the buttons at the top and bottom and the column reads as one raised outline around the track. No line runs across the column, and nothing in it is drawn in the theme's border colour.
The track holds a thumb as tall as the share of the list in view, and never too short to grab, placed as far down the track as the list is scrolled. The thumb is a plain rectangle, as wide as the column, the border and all, with no rounded corners and no bevel, raised over the surface, #222222 on #111111 in dark mode, white laid about 7% of the way over it, so it is brighter than the track. Its top and bottom ends each have a single row of pixels, between the borders, half way between the track and the thumb, #191919 in dark mode, softening where the track meets it. It lightens a step while the pointer is over it, as white laid over it, and another step while it is being dragged, white laid about 3.5% and 7% of the way over it in dark mode, and goes back as soon as neither is true. The thumb never jumps. Its size and place always reflect the whole list's real height, including a list that only draws the rows in view: every row is measured, even those never scrolled into view, so the thumb doesn't grow, shrink, or leap as rows come into view. A row that arrives, or changes, while out of view counts at its height as soon as it does, and after the list's width changes, rewrapping its rows, the height is known in full again by the next frame. Only what has changed is measured again, so a long list stays as quick to scroll and to add to as one that measures only what is in view; only a change of width measures every row again.
A row's height is the same measured out of view as drawn in it. Text in a row, such as a reply's markdown, is parsed once and kept for as long as the app runs, not only while its row is drawn, so a row scrolled away and back is never parsed again, nor shorter for a moment while it is. Long text is parsed in the background, so a row holding it may first measure short: while it parses, its row is measured again every fraction of a second, for a few seconds at most, so the height is right as soon as the parse lands, whether or not the row is in view. 1:# Tasks Tab
3:## How To Build
7:## Theme
11:## Pitch
15:## Description
17:The tab is one scrolling column, with a [Scrollbar](../../scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar), read top to bottom as a timeline, in three groups, each headed by a small muted label with its count: "Previous", every task that has run, oldest at the top, as the [PromptEditor](../../../../scope/prompt-mod
19:All three headings are always in view, however far the tab is scrolled, so each section's controls are always in reach. A heading whose section starts above the visible rows is pinned at the top of the tab, and one whose section starts below them is pinned at its bottom, in their order: scrolled 
22:The list's [Scrollbar](../../scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) is pinned, as every scrollbar is: a column along the tab's right edge, always shown, whether or not the list has anything to scroll, running the tab's full height, from its top to its bottom, beside the pinned headings as well as the rows
24:## Days
27:A day's divider is sticky beneath Previous's own heading: while its tasks are scrolled through, it stays pinned just below that heading, until the next day's divider pushes it out, so the day of the rows in view always shows. Day dividers take the place of the session dividers the previous tasks 
29:## Rows
35:## Virtualized
37:The list is virtualized: however many tasks the project has run, it lays out and draws only the rows in view, and a few rows either side of it, never every row, so opening the tab, scrolling it, resizing the sidebar, filtering, and new tasks arriving cost the same with ten thousand previous tasks
38:A row is drawn only from what its row shows, its mode, status, first line, and time, read from each task's history record once and kept, never by reading a record's output, lines, or snapshots while scrolling; those are read only when a task is opened. Running rows update their time and spinner i
39:Scrolling past either end does nothing: with the list at its top or its bottom, a wheel, trackpad, or drag that goes further leaves every row exactly where it is, frame after frame, with no stretch, bounce, or nudge of even a pixel and back, and draws nothing anew, since nothing moved. Its scroll
40:Scrolled to its bottom, the last row shows whole, its bottom edge at the bottom of the tab's visible area, never cut off by even a pixel, and nothing lies beneath it but the list's own bottom padding of 8 pixels. The list's height is the sum of its rows, headings and day dividers included, and th
42:## Details
51:A long prompt is clipped: past 8 lines, as they wrap at the tab's width, the Prompt section shows its first 8 and fades the last of them into the section's background, with a "Read more" link beneath, in the theme's accent, with a down chevron. Clicking it shows the whole prompt, the link reading
54:## Chain Steps

content.content:
## Description

While the [ChatInput](../chat-input/index.md#chat-input)'s Ask tab is selected, the conversation fills the body's Chat tab, beneath the tab bar and above the chat input, in place of the message list, as the [Body](../../application/Body.md#body) says, never sharing the body with it or with anything else. It goes when another mode's tab is selected, the message list coming back in its place, and comes back as it was, scrolled where it was, when Ask is selected again. Nothing slides as it comes and goes.
It is drawn in the [Theme](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme)'s roles, on the same base surface as the message list. Along its top runs a header 32 pixels tall, on the tab bar's background with the theme's line beneath it, reading "Questions" at its left, with 12 pixels of padding, and at its right how many questions it holds, muted. Beneath it, the conversation spans the full width of the space it fills, from the body's left edge to its right, or to the right sidebar while it is there, its questions and answers laid out across all of it with only its own padding at either side, never set in a narrower column, centred or not, and never leaving empty space beside it. It widens and narrows with the body as the window or a sidebar is resized.

35:Some of it belongs to one machine rather than to the project: the harness report `.suspense/harness.json`, the fluency `.suspense/fluency.md`, printed by this machine's piton, the Suspense fluency `.suspense/suspense-fluency.md`, written by this machine's Suspense, the queue `.suspense/queue/`, the commit notes `.suspense/commit-notes.json`, the conversations left `.suspense/conversations.json`, whose conversations only this machine's harness knows, the harness's sessions `.suspense/sessions/`, which hold its transcripts, the snapshot index `.suspense/snapshot-index`, and the draft `.suspense-draft.pi` wherever it is, should it ever be written. Git ignores these, so they are never committed. Everything else, the prompt history, the questions, the divergence reports, the system prompts, and the project's Containerfile, is kept with the project.
38:## Task Snapshots
40:In a project that is a git repository, every task the harness runs keeps a record of the files that changed while it ran. When the harness actually starts the task, not when it is sent or queued, the project's working tree is snapshotted, and it is snapshotted again when the run is over, however it ends: done, failed, or cancelled. In a project that isn't a git repository, nothing is snapshotted or recorded, and nothing about it is shown anywhere.
41:A snapshot is a git tree, made with git's plumbing alone: `git add -A` and then `git write-tree`, run with `GIT_INDEX_FILE` pointing at a private index, `.suspense/snapshot-index`, so the repository's own index, HEAD, branches, stash, and working tree are never read from or written to. The private index is kept between snapshots, so each one hashes again only the files whose timestamps changed since the last. A snapshot follows `.gitignore`, as git does, so ignored files, `.suspense`'s machine-only data among them, are never in it. No commit, branch, worktree, or stash is ever made, nothing is added to the user's history, and no tool but git is needed.
42:Both trees are pinned so git's garbage collection never deletes them, each under a private ref, `refs/suspense/<task>/before` and `refs/suspense/<task>/after`, `<task>` being the task's hidden anchor's name, and their hashes are kept in the task's history record. A snapshot that can't be taken, as when git fails, is left out rather than stopping the task; a task missing either snapshot shows no changed files.
43:The private index and the refs belong to this machine: `snapshot-index` is ignored by git like the other machine-only data, and the refs are never pushed, since nothing pushes `refs/suspense/`.
13:A file's status is one of modified, added, untracked, conflicted, or ignored; an unchanged file has none. A renamed file counts as modified. Everything inside an ignored folder is ignored too. A folder takes the most pressing status among its contents, conflicted first, then modified, added, and untracked.
17:Modified is amber, added green, untracked teal, and conflicted red, each a shade readable in both the light and the dark theme. Ignored is dimmed.

Task snapshots now cover only the project directory. When the project is a subfolder of a larger repository, files outside it are no longer snapshotted or listed among a task's changed files.

- **Snapshots:** they are still built with `git add -A` against the private index, but now only on the project's own folder. The first snapshot after this change drops any outside files an older snapshot had put in that index.
- **Changed files:** the list is limited to the project folder too. So a task whose first snapshot was taken before this change, while it was still running, doesn't show outside files as deleted.
- **Git status:** this part already worked, so I only added a test for it. `git status --ignored=matching` already reports an ignored folder as one entry (`target/` or `build/`, not every file inside it), and the project tree already dims everything within it.

The new tests pass: one for snapshots in a subfolder project, and a check that an ignored folder is a single entry.

In the full suite, the same 14 tests as before fail because your uncommitted spec rename broke them (`ApplicationScope` is now `Application`). `quitting_while_a_task_runs_asks_first` also failed in the full run but passed twice on its own.

31:Every task is one row, 28 pixels tall, as a queued prompt's is, and every row in every section is laid out in the same columns, so their parts line up down the whole list: a bar in its mode's colour, as the [PromptModes](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes) colours it, 4 pixels wide with corners rounded 2 pixels, inset from the row's edges, 4 pixels from its left and 6 from its top and bottom, so it stands as a short rounded pill rather than running edge to edge, and the bars of rows one above another never touch; then a lead column 20 pixels wide, holding a Previous row's checkbox, a Queued row's drag grip, and nothing in a Running row, the column kept empty rather than closed up where there is nothing in it; then a status column 20 pixels wide, a spinner while it is under way, a tick, cross, or dash once it has ended, or, queued, its place in the queue; then the first line of its prompt, cut off with an ellipsis; then, at its right, muted, how long it took, or has been running, as the [MessageList](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list) writes it, right-aligned in a column of its own, and any buttons the row has after it. So a row's status and its text start at the same place whether it has a checkbox, a grip, or neither, and so do the section headings' titles, set in from their chevrons to line up with the rows' text.
32:A chain, or any task of more than one step, is one row like any other, its status the chain's as a whole, with its step count muted beside its time. In Previous and Queued its steps are never listed in the list; they are shown once it is opened, as its chain steps say. While it is Running, it is expanded in the Running group: its row, then a row for each of its steps beneath it, in the order they run, sent or still to send, each a 28 pixel row in the same columns, its text set in 16 pixels further and labelled "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up" in that step's mode colour, with the step's own status, a tick, cross, or dash for one that has ended, a spinner for the one running, "Queued" with its place in its lane's queue for one waiting there, and a muted "Next" for one that will be sent once the step before it finishes, and "Waiting" for any after that, every step listed from the moment the chain is sent, as its chain steps say, each with its own time. A step being queued shows here, as part of its chain, rather than among the queued prompts, though it keeps its place in its lane's queue. The steps can't be collapsed, and once the chain is over they go with it into Previous as a single row. Clicking the chain's row, or any of its steps, opens the chain, its Steps section showing the same.
33:A chain's rows are joined by its colour: in place of each row's own bar, one bar in the Chain colour, purple, 4 pixels wide with corners rounded 2 pixels, runs unbroken down the left of the chain's row and every step row beneath it, Spec, Code, Spec follow-up, and any step added, from 6 pixels below the top of the chain's row to 6 pixels above the bottom of its last step's, across the gaps between the rows, so the chain reads as one block. The steps' own modes show in their labels' colours, never in a bar of their own. It is drawn the same in a chain's Steps section once opened, and grows or shrinks with the chain as a step is added. A single task, not part of a chain, keeps its own bar. Clicking a row opens it, as below, and the row stays highlighted while it is open. Hovering a row shows its prompt's first lines in its tooltip.
37:The list is virtualized: however many tasks the project has run, it lays out and draws only the rows in view, and a few rows either side of it, never every row, so opening the tab, scrolling it, resizing the sidebar, filtering, and new tasks arriving cost the same with ten thousand previous tasks as with ten. Every row is 28 pixels tall, section headings included, so where each row lies is known from its place in the list alone, without laying out the rows before it, and the scrollbar's thumb is sized and placed from the whole list's height, as though every row were drawn.
38:A row is drawn only from what its row shows, its mode, status, first line, and time, read from each task's history record once and kept, never by reading a record's output, lines, or snapshots while scrolling; those are read only when a task is opened. Running rows update their time and spinner in place, redrawing only what is in view. Scrolling to a row, as when the tab opens on Running, a filter changes, or a queued row is dragged past the edge, jumps straight to its place without drawing the rows between. A row scrolled out of view and back is the same as it was, its selection and highlight kept. A pinned heading sits over the list without moving any row, so where each row lies is unchanged by it.
39:Scrolling past either end does nothing: with the list at its top or its bottom, a wheel, trackpad, or drag that goes further leaves every row exactly where it is, frame after frame, with no stretch, bounce, or nudge of even a pixel and back, and draws nothing anew, since nothing moved. A list scrolled to its bottom stays at its bottom as rows are added, and one at its top stays at its top. content.content:
## Details

An open task takes the tab's place, with a back arrow and the task's mode and name along its top, the arrow and <Escape> going back to the list as it was left. Opening a task that has run or is running also opens it in a tab of its own in the body, as a file opens, as the [Body](../../../../scope/application/Body.md#body) says, showing its header and output there, unless it is a task the Chat tab shows, one running or the one it shows while none runs, when Chat is selected instead, with that task selected in its header. What the open task shows, top to bottom:
- Status: its status label and how long it took, or has been running, as the MessageList writes them, on one line
- Prompt: its prompt, as it was typed, in a GrowingTextInput, and beneath it what is attached to it
- Steps: for a chain, its steps, as its chain steps say, with Add step; a task that isn't a chain has no Steps section
- Details: the rest at a glance, its lane, its place in the queue while it waits, the conversation it carries on or that it starts a new one, its model and effort, and once it has run, how many tool calls it made, its errors, its tokens and their cost, and how many files it changed, each a labelled figure, those that don't apply left out
- Parameters: its mode, its model and effort, its Slice toggle, and whether it starts a new conversation, each as the chat input shows it
- Actions: Resend, Send to Spec or Send to Code, Pause while it runs or Resume while it is paused, Cancel while it is under way, paused, or queued, and Open output, as the PromptSending gives them
 A step not yet sent can be edited, moved among the others not yet sent, or removed; one sent reads as it was.

Its tooltip says how it was worked out, "Output tokens over time waiting on the model" or "Output tokens over time writing, as measured". A rate the harness gives too little to work out, as a run that reported no output tokens, or took no measurable time, is left out rather than shown as zero.

content.content:
### Description

A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green, "Failed" in red, "Cancelled" in orange, "Paused" in the theme's warning colour for a task paused to be resumed, as the PromptSending says, "Stopped" in grey for a chain that stopped short of a step it was to run, and "Not recorded" in grey for a task from the history with no record of its run. The labels are readable in both light and dark mode.

### Elapsed

Beside its status label, a task shows how long it has been under way, from when it was sent, building and compiling included, in small muted tabular figures: minutes and seconds, "0:42" or "12:05", with hours ahead of them once it reaches an hour, "1:02:33". While the task is building, compiling, or running, it counts up every second, so a task that seems stuck can be told from one that has only just started. Once the task is over, however it ended, it stops and stays at how long the task took. It shows wherever the status label does, the latest task's header and the heading of each previous task, including a task running in the other lane. A task from the history whose record holds no start and end, as one recorded before they were kept, shows how long it took as well as can be told, from the second its history file is named by to when its record was written, with "≈" before it, as "≈ 4:12", its tooltip saying it is approximate; one where neither can be told shows none.
Among the previous tasks, every task's heading shows how long it took, as the latest task's header does, though not beside its status: done, failed, or cancelled alike, and a task still running there counting up. A chain's parent row shows the time its steps took together, from when its first step was sent to when its last ended, and each step's heading beneath it its own. The times line up, right-aligned in their own column of the heading, just before its buttons, so the list reads as a column of durations that can be compared at a glance, and a long one stands out.

content.content:
## Answers

While an answer is being written, its status line shows the output rate beside it, and once it is over, a small muted line at its foot gives its average output rate, as the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list)'s status says of a task.
An answer is not drawn as a [TaskTable](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table): it has no columns, no Type badges or Status labels, and no lines between rows. What is shown is the answer's reply text, the reply rows after the harness's last tool call, as the table's collapsed steps count them, rendered as markdown in the body's text colour, one paragraph after another, as a message in a chat is. Code blocks, lists, tables, and links in it are rendered as markdown renders them anywhere. An answer with no tool calls is all reply text; a finished answer with nothing to show reads "No answer.", muted.
Everything the harness did before the answer, its tool calls and any reply text between them, is gathered into one line above the answer, small and muted, beside a right chevron, summing it up, as "Read 3 files, searched twice, ran 1 command" or "Worked through 6 steps" where it can't be summed up by kind. Clicking it expands the steps in place, beneath it and above the answer, as compact muted lines, one per step: a tool call as its tool's name, muted, then its most telling argument, shortened as the [TaskTable](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table)'s tool calls are, and reply text between them as muted markdown; clicking it again collapses them. It starts collapsed, and stays as it was left for as long as the application runs. An answer whose harness did nothing before replying has no such line.
While the harness works on a question, a status line takes that line's place: a spinner and the latest thing the harness did, muted, with a Stop button at its right that stops just that question, leaving the others running. Reply text streams in beneath it as prose as the harness writes it; text it goes on to follow with a tool call joins the steps once the call comes, so only the answer is left as prose. Once the question finishes, the status line becomes the summary line.
A question that failed ends its answer with the error, in the theme's error colour, beneath whatever reply came before it. One that was stopped ends with "Stopped", muted. Neither is shown as a status in a table.
Questions are 16 pixels apart, and a question's answer 8 pixels beneath it.
Questions asked while another is still running come in at the bottom in the order they were asked, each answered in its own place as its harness goes, so answers can be filling in at once.

## Suggested Prompts

14://! rows of it, its box, its summary or status line, each step shown, each
88:    /// the run is on its last segment, its status line; nothing when there
145:    /// The last segment, which a running prompt's status line heads.
730:                // While it runs, its status line follows the harness.

content.text:
Runs now show how fast the harness is writing, and the new tests for it pass.

- **While writing:** the task header shows a live rate beside the elapsed time, muted, such as "42 tok/s". A question's status line shows the same. None of the harnesses report output tokens mid-reply, so the live rate is always an estimate: about four characters per token, smoothed over the last 3 seconds. It disappears while a tool call is running and before the reply begins.
- **When it's over:** the task header shows the run's average rate, and an answer shows it in a small muted line at its foot. The tooltip says which method was used:
  - **Claude Code:** output tokens over the time spent waiting on the model, taken from Claude Code's reported API time.
  - **Other harnesses:** output tokens over the time Suspense measured from each turn's start to its usage report, with tool calls left out. That measured time is now saved in the task's history record, so the average still shows after a restart.
- **Usage popover:** the Conversation and This project groups each have an "Output rate" row.
- **Unknown rates:** a rate with no output tokens or no time is left out, never shown as zero.

Claude Code's reported API time is a running total for the whole conversation, not just the current run. So each run's share is worked out as the rise since the conversation's previous run, the same way its tokens already are.

The new code is mainly in a new file, `src/output_rate.rs`, plus `src/usage.rs` and the header and answer views.

The full suite has 16 failures. 14 are the ones broken by your uncommitted spec rename. The other two, `podman_failing_is_said_plainly` and `long_output_is_measured_a_few_rows_a_frame`, passed both times I re-ran them on their own.

content.content:
## Panel

It has no header: its contents start at its top edge, on the theme's base surface.
It shows no count of what it lists.
It fills the height its sidebar's other panels leave.
Its contents scroll on their own when they are taller than it, with a permanent scrollbar along its right, as the Scrollbar says.

## Pitch
## Look

The panel's top row, the branch, is its header: 32 pixels tall, on the ribbon's tab row colour, #333333 in dark mode. Beneath it, the panel's body is on the ribbon's command area colour, #222222 in dark mode, with 8 pixels of padding at either side and at the bottom, and 4 pixels between one thing and the next. There is no line between the header and the body, nor between the file tree and the header: the change of colour is the edge. The header has, along its bottom, the 1 pixel border in the body's colour, #222222 in dark mode, that every panel header has, as the [Sidebar](../sidebar/index.md#sidebar) says. Every box and button in it is square, with no rounded corners and no border, and the Pull and Push buttons are square too.

## Sizing

57:- Git: the GitPanel alone, filling the view, its changes list taking the height the git panel's own sections leave, no longer squeezed beneath the file tree
60:The Git panel and the file tree no longer share a view: the edge that was dragged between them is gone, and each view has the whole height. Everything else about each panel stays as its own spec says.

# Ribbon Planning Tab

## How To Build

A RibbonPlanningTab should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A RibbonPlanningTab should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, integration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [Theme](../../../theme/index.md#theme): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Pitch

The ribbon's Planning tab: the commands for planning work before it is sent, to be added.

## Description

The Planning tab of the ribbon, between Project and Code. It takes no mode's colour: its label is in the tab row's own colour, as Project's and Application's are.

## Groups

None yet. Opened alone, the command area reads "No commands yet", as the ribbon says of a tab with no commands, and opened beside other tabs, it adds nothing to the command area.
18:A tab whose commands work on one of the chat input's modes, as the Code and Spec tabs do, takes that mode's colour: its label is in the mode's colour while the tab is closed, and while open, the tab is tinted with it instead and its label is the tab's own colour. Each such tab says more. Its tabs are, in order: Project, Planning, Code, Spec, and Application. The window always opens on Project. Beneath the tabs, the selected tab's commands sit in groups. There is no raw output view and no toggle for one.
22:<Alt+1> opens the first tab, <Alt+2> the second, and so on, through each tab in the order the tabs are shown, <Alt+2> opening Planning and <Alt+5> Application. Each opens its tab alone, as clicking it does, and expands the ribbon first if it is collapsed. A number past the last tab does nothing. Like the ribbon's other shortcuts, they do nothing while an inset panel is open. A tab's tooltip doesn't give its shortcut, since a tab has no tooltip.

content.content:
## Time Breakdown

An open task that has started, and an open chain or step, has a Time section, beneath its Steps, or its Prompt where it has none, and above its Details, showing where its time went, so what is slow can be seen at a glance: waiting on the model, building the spec, running commands, and the rest.
Its time is split into kinds, each with a colour of its own, drawn from the theme's chart colours, distinct from one another in light and dark mode and never a mode's colour, so a kind looks the same in every task:
- Queued: waiting in its lane's queue before it was sent
- Spec build: building the spec ahead of it, and after it for a spec step
- Preparing: building or starting its container, and the snapshots taken as it started and ended
- Model: the harness waiting on the model, thinking and writing, between tool calls
- Commands: shell commands it ran and waited on, a build or tests among them
- Files: reading, searching, and editing files
- Subagents: subagents it waited on
- Web: fetching and searching the web
- Other: any other tool call, and time that fits none of these
Each kind's time is worked out from the times its record keeps, as the [ProjectData](../../../../scope/project-data/index.md#project-data) says: each phase from its start to its end, and each tool call from when it was made to when its result came, counted as its kind; Model is the time between, from each turn's start, or a tool call's result, to the next tool call or the turn's end. A subagent's own tool calls count as Subagents, not as their own kinds, and background tasks that ran beside the main thread are never counted twice: only the time the task itself waited on them. Time while paused is left out, as is the gap between a chain's steps.
Along the top of the section, a single bar, the section's full width and 12 pixels tall, with corners rounded 3 pixels, split into a segment per kind in the order above, each as wide as its share of the whole, a pixel of the section's surface between segments, kinds with no time left out. Beneath it, a legend, one line per kind with time, in order of the time it took, largest first: a square of its colour, its name, its time, as the [MessageList](../../../../scope/prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list) writes times, and its share, muted, as "Model 4:12 · 61%". The largest is in the theme's text colour and the rest muted, so what took longest stands out. Hovering a segment, or its legend line, lightens the other segments and shows a tooltip giving the kind's time, its share, and, for Commands, Files, Subagents, and Web, how many calls and the slowest of them, as "npm run build, 1:38".
Beneath the legend, a timeline of the task from start to end, the section's full width and 24 pixels tall: each phase and tool call as a bar at its place along it, in its kind's colour, so long waits and when they came can be seen, with a muted time at either end. Hovering a bar names what it was and how long it took, and clicking a tool call's bar opens the task's output scrolled to that row.
While the task runs, the section follows it, the kind under way growing in place and the timeline extending to now. A chain's Time section shows its steps' time together, the bar split by kind across all of them, and the timeline marking where each step began; each step's own section shows its own. A task from before its phases were kept shows only its total time, muted, saying its breakdown wasn't recorded.
48:- Time: where its time went, as its time breakdown says, once it has started
57:An open Chain task lists its steps in its Steps section, beneath its prompt and above its details, in the order they run, each a row as in the list, with its status: its spec step, its code step, and its spec follow-up when it has one. Every step it will run is listed from the moment the chain is sent, while its spec step is still building or running, before any later step has been sent: a step
61:An open task that has started, and an open chain or step, has a Time section, beneath its Steps, or its Prompt where it has none, and above its Details, showing where its time went, so what is slow can be seen at a glance: waiting on the model, building the spec, running commands, and the rest.
## Chart Colours

The theme has a set of chart colours, for anything that tells kinds apart in a chart, such as a task's time breakdown: nine hues, in a fixed order, blue, amber, teal, violet, rose, lime, sky, orange, and a neutral grey for "other", each readable on the theme's surfaces in both dark and light mode, set apart from one another in lightness as well as hue so they can still be told apart by someone who can't tell some hues apart, and distinct from the modes' colours and the status colours, so a chart is never read as a mode or a state. They follow the theme's brightness as its other colours do. A chart takes them in order and keeps each kind to the same colour wherever it is shown.
