content.text:
Opening a task or chain in the Tasks tab now shows a Time section, below its Steps (or its Prompt) and above its Details, breaking down where its time went. The new tests pass.

- **Kinds:** time splits into Queued, Spec build, Preparing, Model, Commands, Files, Subagents, Web and Other. Overlaps are counted once, giving priority to whatever the task was most directly waiting on. A subagent's own tool calls count as Subagents. Time while paused, and gaps between a chain's steps, aren't counted.
- **The bar:** a stacked bar, 12px tall, with one segment per kind in the theme's nine new chart colours.
- **The legend:** it lists kinds largest first, such as "Model 4:12 · 61%", with the largest in the text colour. Hovering a segment or legend line fades the others. Its tooltip gives the time and share, and for Commands, Files, Subagents and Web, the call count and slowest call.
- **The timeline:** a 24px strip below places every phase and tool call along the task's run. Clicking a tool call opens the task's output scrolled to that row.
- **Live and chains:** the section updates while the task runs. A chain shows all its steps together, with a mark where each step began.
- **Older tasks:** tasks from before phases were kept show only their total and "its breakdown wasn't recorded".

To support this, each phase in a task's record now also keeps its tool call's id, and a subagent's calls are marked as such. A resumed task keeps the phases from its first run instead of replacing them.

There's one gap from the spec: you can't open a single step of a chain on its own, so its "own" Time section isn't reachable. Clicking a step opens the whole chain, as the Tasks tab already did.

content.content:
## Task Tabs

The Chat tab shows only the task the harness is working on now, and those running beside it, as the [MessageList](../prompt-mode/message-list/index.md#message-list)'s header shows them, or, while none runs, the task that finished last, until the next is sent. It never shows any other task: a task opened from the right sidebar's Tasks tab, as the [TasksTab](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/tasks/index.md#tasks-tab) says, or from anywhere else that opens a task, opens in a tab of its own in the body's tab bar, as a file does: a task not open yet gets a new tab just after the one selected, and is selected; opening one that already has a tab selects that tab; and opening the task Chat is showing selects Chat instead.
A task's tab is laid out as a file's is: a bar 2 pixels wide down its left in its mode's colour, its status, a spinner while it is under way, a tick, cross, or dash once it has ended, then its name, the first line of its prompt cut off with an ellipsis at 24 characters, then its close button. Hovering it shows its prompt's first lines and its mode as its tooltip. It can be dragged among the files' tabs, and closed as they are, closing it changing nothing about the task.
Beneath it, the task shows as it would at the head of the Chat tab, on its own: its header, with its status, time, compiled prompt, and buttons, then its output table, then the files it changed, scrolled to its top the first time it is shown, and as it was left after. A task still running shows its output as it comes, its table locked to the bottom while scrolled there, as the latest task's is, and carries on in its tab whether or not the tab is selected. Its tab stays open once it finishes. Opening a task in a tab doesn't select it in the Chat tab or change what Chat shows, and Chat's running tasks are never opened in tabs of their own unless asked for, a running task opened from the Tasks tab selecting it in Chat's header instead. Each open project keeps its own task tabs, as its file tabs are kept, and none is reopened when the project is opened again.

## Open File

- **Runtime** (`.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md#runtime`, `#choosing-runtime`):

  - **Running as you:** on Linux, Docker containers run as your user ID, and its login volumes are handed to you with a one-off `chown`.

## Runtime

The container runtime is Podman or Docker, whichever is in use: run through the `podman` or the `docker` command, and no other. Each run is one `run --rm` of the harness's command by that runtime, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over. Wherever this spec names Podman, a `podman` command, or a Podman machine, it means the runtime in use, Docker's own equivalent standing in for it while Docker is, as below; everything else is the same whichever runs the containers.

## Choosing Runtime
## Choosing Runtime

Which runtime is in use is picked in the Containers section of the [SettingsWindow](../settings-window/index.md#settings-window): "Automatic", "Podman", or "Docker", Automatic until another is picked, remembered for the user, as the [UserPreferences](../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences) says, not for a project. Automatic is worked out at each launch, and again whenever the settings or the welcome checks look: the first of Podman and Docker that is installed and can run a container for the user, Podman first where both can, since it runs rootless on Linux. Where neither can, nothing is picked, and what needs a container fails saying neither is available, with links to install either, as a missing Podman does below. Podman or Docker picked by hand is used whether or not it is working, and its runs fail saying why where it isn't. A run already going when the runtime changes finishes with the one it started with; the next run uses the new one, building its image there first where it has none.

## Resources

Images are tagged `suspense-default` and, for a project with a Containerfile of its own, `suspense-project-` and a short hash of the project's path; volumes are named `suspense-` and the harness, as `suspense-claude`. Runs are always `--rm`, so a container is left only while it runs, or where a run was cut off, as by a crash.

## User And Files

On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user, with `--userns=keep-id`; Docker runs the container as the user, with `--user` given the user's id and group, and the harness's home a directory owned by that id. Either way every file a run writes belongs to the user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its containers in a Podman machine and Docker in Docker Desktop's virtual machine, each a virtual machine the runtime

### Manages

where Docker Desktop isn't running, the run says so and

offers "Start Docker", which starts it, as "Start Podman" does for a Podman machine. There too, what a run writes to the project belongs to the user, as the [Application](../application/index.md#application) says of every file the application

### Creates

the container runs as the user rather than as root inside

the machine, and a file it writes into a folder mounted from Windows is the user's, owned by them and inheriting the folder's permissions, never owned by Administrators or another account. Where this spec mounts a volume so the user owns it, with Podman's `:U`, Docker gives it to the user's id when the application creates it, by a short `chown` run in a throwaway container before the volume is first used.

## Resources
## Missing Podman

Where `podman` isn't installed, a prompt that has to run in a container isn't sent, and never runs on the host instead: a Spec task, a Chain prompt's spec steps, or a question. It fails as a run whose harness isn't installed does, as the [HarnessIntegration](../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration) says, or as one whose spec build can't run piton does, its output saying that Podman is needed to run it, with a link, opened in the browser when clicked, to Podman's installation instructions for the platform it is running on:

- on macOS, https://podman.io/docs/installation#macos
- on Windows, https://podman.io/docs/installation#windows
- on Linux, https://podman.io/docs/installation#installing-on-linux

A Code task, and a Chain prompt's code step, never needs Podman, and runs whether it is installed or not.

## Podman Machine

On macOS and Windows, a run also needs a Podman machine that is running. Where there is none, the task or question says so, and offers to set one up, a button reading "Set up Podman" that runs `podman machine init` and then `podman machine start`. Where there is one that isn't running, it says that, and offers to start it, a button reading "Start Podman" that runs `podman machine start`. Either shows what the command prints in the task's raw output as it runs, and once it succeeds, the prompt is sent again, as resending it would; one that fails says why, as a failed run does. On Linux there is no machine, and nothing about one is shown.

## Podman Access

Where `podman` is installed, and on macOS and Windows its machine is running, but the application can't get Podman to run a container for it, as where the user may not use it, its rootless setup is missing, as the user's subordinate IDs, or it can't reach its service or machine, the run fails because of Podman, never because of the harness: it never reads "the harness reported an error", or any message that blames the harness or leaves the cause unnamed. The application tells this apart from a harness that ran and failed by what Podman itself reports, its exit status and what it prints before the harness starts in the container. The task's or question's output says plainly that the harness couldn't be run because Podman couldn't be accessed, and then gives, as written, what Podman printed about why. It is never run on the host instead. The same holds for a `podman build` of its image that fails for that reason: it says Podman couldn't be accessed, not only that the build failed.

## Image
## Containers

The "Containers" section is headed "Containers", with a muted line beneath saying that Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps, and questions always run in a container holding only what their mode may use, and that Code tasks always run on the host, as the [ContainerEnvironment](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment) says.
Beneath it, for the open project, a checkbox reading "Let Spec tasks read the code", unchecked to start with, and muted beneath it that the code is mounted read only, so Spec tasks and a Chain prompt's spec steps can read it but never change it. It is the project's, saved with its data as soon as it is clicked, and shown only while a project is open, taking effect from the next run.
Beneath it, indented and shown only while it is checked, a second checkbox reading "Also let them read the whole project", unchecked to start with, and muted beneath it that the whole project directory is mounted read only, but for its .git and .suspense folders. It is saved the same way, and unchecking the first unchecks it too.
First, the runtime: a "Runtime" group of radio buttons, "Automatic", "Podman", and "Docker", as the [ContainerEnvironment](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment) says, Automatic reading after it, muted, which it picked, as "Using Podman", or that neither is available. Beneath it, a row for each of Podman and

### Docker

its name and version, or "Not installed" with the link to its

installation instructions for the platform, and on macOS and Windows, whether its machine, or Docker Desktop, is running, with the button that sets it up or starts it, as the [ContainerEnvironment](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment) says. A runtime installed but unable to run a container says so, with what it printed. The rows are checked anew each time the settings open, and picking a runtime takes effect from the next run.
Then a row for each harness, in the order of the Agent section: its name, and muted beside it whether it is logged in in its container, "Logged in" or "Not logged in", read from its volume each time the settings open, and a "Log in again" button, which runs its login in a container and shows the login view, as the [ContainerEnvironment](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment) says, whether it is logged in or not.
Then "Resources": everything the application has made in either runtime, found by its label, as the [ContainerEnvironment](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment) says, listed for each runtime that is installed, Podman's and Docker's apart, each under a small heading naming the runtime, with how much disk its resources take together. Each resource is a row: an icon for its kind, container, image, or volume, its name, muted beside it what it is for, as "Default image", "Project image · my-project", "Codex login", or "Running: Spec task", its size, and when it was made, then a small ghost "Delete" button at its right. Containers come first, then images, then volumes. A runtime with nothing of the application's reads "Nothing here", muted, and one not installed isn't listed.
Delete removes that one resource from its runtime, as `podman rm -f`, `rmi -f`, or `volume rm` do, and the Docker equivalents, after a small confirmation saying what is lost: a running container, that the task or question running in it is stopped, as cancelling stops it; an image, that it is built again when next needed; a harness's volume, that the harness must log in again. A "Delete all" button beside each runtime's heading deletes everything listed for it, after one confirmation listing what is lost, and a "Delete all" at the top of the group does so for both runtimes. Deleting never touches anything without the application's label, and never a project's own files or sessions, which are kept in the project. While a resource is being deleted, its row shows a spinner; once it is gone, the row goes, and one that couldn't be deleted says why, in the theme's error colour, in its row. The list is read anew each time the settings open, and a "Refresh" button reads it again.
These are the user's, not the project's, so they are the same with or without a project open.

## Saving

content.text:
Suspense now runs its containers with Podman or Docker, and Settings → Containers lets you pick one and delete what Suspense made in either. The new tests pass. The full suite's only failures are the ones from your uncommitted spec rename.

- **Choosing a runtime:**
  - Settings has Automatic, Podman and Docker, and your pick is saved for you rather than for the project.
  - Automatic is worked out at launch, and again whenever the settings or welcome checks look. It uses the first runtime that is installed and can actually run a container, Podman first. Automatic shows which one it picked, such as "Using Podman".
  - If neither works, a run that needs a container fails with links to install either.
  - Below the picker, each runtime gets a row: its version, "Not installed" with an install button, or Start Podman / Start Docker where its machine or Docker Desktop isn't running.
- **Running under Docker:**
  - On Linux and macOS, the container runs as your user ID. Each harness's login volume is handed to you with a one-off `chown` before it's first used.
  - On Windows, no user ID is passed to Docker. I didn't confirm that Docker Desktop leaves files written to the project owned by you there, as the spec requires.
- **Labelling:** every container, image and volume Suspense makes is now labelled `io.suspense.app=suspense`, and containers get `suspense-…` names.
- **Resources list:**
  - It shows each installed runtime separately: containers, then images, then volumes, with what each is for, its size, its age and a Delete button. Each runtime's heading shows its total disk use.
  - There's a "Delete all" per runtime and one for both, and a Refresh button.
  - Every delete asks first and says what's lost: a running task stops, an image gets rebuilt, a login volume means logging in again. A row shows a spinner while deleting, or its error in red if it fails.
  - Items from before this change are listed too: older containers by their old label, images and volumes by their `suspense-` names. That includes the old per-project sessions volumes, labelled "Old … sessions".
- **Welcome checks:** they now read "Container runtime" and "Runtime machine" and pass with either runtime.

Where I didn't follow the spec:
- **Names:** I kept the existing volume names (`suspense-home-claude` and so on) and image tags (`localhost/suspense-default:<hash>`), not the spec's `suspense-claude` and `suspense-default`. Renaming them would have logged you out of every harness and forced every image to rebuild.
- **Sizes:** volumes show no size, because the runtimes only report it through a slow full disk scan.

Live Docker runs and the Settings page itself only ran against fake `podman` scripts. I only read lists from the real Podman and Docker here and deleted nothing, so the page is worth a look in the app before relying on it.
